blocks.description: Which families of typographic substitution apply when the text of a document is resolved (curly quotes, dashes, ellipses). Fixed when the registry is built: it cannot vary per document or per render.

auto_unicode_quotes.description:
Whether the straight double quote `"` and the straight single quote `'`
become curly quotes, opening (`“`, `‘`) or closing (`”`, `’`) according
to their position. When
`ligature_unicode_quotes` is
also on, the two-character ligature `''` is that family's, and this test
applies to a single `'`.

A quote opens at the start of a text run that no content precedes (a
comment does not count, nor the spaces `~` and `\ `), and after
whitespace, an opening bracket
(`(`, `[`, `{`) or a dash (`-`, `–`, `—`). A single quote also opens
before a digit (`x'9` becomes `x‘9`), except in a decade abbreviation:
after a letter, a digit or an underscore, and before two digits and an
`s` (`x'90s` becomes
`x’90s`). A quote closes everywhere else: `don't` becomes `don’t`. The
test looks at the node before the text run, so in `\(A_j\)'s` the quote
after the formula closes.

ligature_unicode_quotes.description:
Whether the TeX quote ligatures apply: ``` `` ``` becomes `“`, `''`
becomes `”`, and `` ` `` becomes `‘`. A single `'` becomes `’`, as in
TeX, only when `auto_unicode_quotes` is
off; when both families are on, the position test of
`auto_unicode_quotes` decides a single `'`.

ligature_unicode_dashes.description:
Whether the TeX dash ligatures apply: `---` becomes an em dash `—` and
`--` an en dash `–`.

ligature_unicode_ellipses.description: Whether the ellipsis ligature applies: `...` becomes `…`.

BlocksConfig.description:
The options of text resolution in the block-structure pass: one
flag per family of typographic substitutions. Collapsing whitespace always
happens and has no flag.

Every family is on by default, so that FLM source written with the usual TeX
spellings (`` `quoted' ``, `--`, `...`) is shown as its author meant it in
every output format. Switch a family off to have those spellings reach the
output unchanged.

A value is passed to `structure`, or to the `blocks`
feature's constructor
(`Blocks::new`). Because
every field is public, a value can be built from the default with one change,
or from `no_typography` with one family
switched on. In settings written as data (`crate::core::settings`), the
fields are the settings keys of the `blocks` feature, and a key left out
takes its default.

numbering.description:
The counter styles that replace declared ones: each entry replaces, by its name, the counter style a feature declares. Fixed when the registry is built: it cannot vary per document or per render.

Per counter, the counter it is numbered within and the value it has before it is first advanced. Set on the document; a render request may set it again, and its value then replaces the document's for that render.

styles.description:
The replacements, each replacing the counter style declaration of the
same name, in the order they were given.

An entry in data gives only the fields it changes; every other field
takes the value that `CounterStyleDecl::new` gives, not the declared
counter style's value, so a replacement restates every field it keeps.

counters.description: What the document says about each counter it mentions, in name order.

styles.description:
The replacements, each replacing the counter style declaration of the
same name, in the order they were given.

An entry in data gives only the fields it changes; every other field
takes the value that `CounterStyleDecl::new` gives, not the declared
counter style's value, so a replacement restates every field it keeps.

NumberingConfig.description:
The configuration of the `numbering` feature: the counter styles
that a host replaces.

A counter style (`CounterStyleDecl`) is declared by the feature that
numbers with it. A host that wants other words before a number, another
number format or other delimiters gives a replacement: a whole counter
style declaration with the same name, which takes the place of the
declared one. It is how a host changes the words, the number template or
the delimiters of a counter style without writing a feature. A document's
numbering options (`NumberingOptions`) change
only what a counter is numbered within and how the numbers of those
counters are written before its own, and a reference point may give a
number template of its own in its number source
(`NumberSource::number_format`).
A replacement for a counter style that no feature declares fails the
registry build, so a misspelled name is reported once instead of changing
nothing.

The configuration is fixed when the registry is built (settings, options
and configuration),
because every text of a counter style is parsed then. A host passes it as
the `numbering` field of `StdcoreConfig`,
or in data as the `styles` settings key, a map from a counter style's name
to its replacement. An entry in data gives only the fields it changes;
every other field takes the value that `CounterStyleDecl::new` gives (a
decimal number, no word, no delimiters, the default join texts), not the
declared counter style's value, so a replacement restates every field it
keeps.

number_format.description: The number template: how the number itself is written.

sub_levels.description:
The sub-levels, outermost first. A value cannot be written with a
sub-number at a level the counter style does not declare.

prefix_words.description: The prefix words: the word written before the number.

delimiters.description: The delimiters: the texts around the number.

join.description: The join texts: the texts that join several numbers.

name_in_link.description:
Whether the word before the numbers is part of the link to the first
number written. With one number written by `format()`, the whole
text is one link regardless of this setting. On by default.

repeat_parents_in_range.description:
Whether the end of a range repeats the part of the number that comes
from the counters it is numbered within: `A.I–A.III` instead of
`A.I–III`. Off by default.

ranges.description:
Whether consecutive numbers collapse into a range: `1–3` when on,
`1,2,3` when off. Several numbers are sorted in both cases, and when
off every number is written separately, each with a link of its own.
On by default.

number_writer.description:
The name of the number writer that writes this
counter style's numbers, registered under that name in
`NUMBER_WRITERS_SLOT`, or `None` for the
default writer. A name no feature registers fails the registry build.

CounterStyleDecl.description:
A counter style, as a feature declares it.

A counter style says how a counter value is shown: the number template, the
sub-levels, the prefix words with their variants, the delimiters and the
join texts, each text written in FLM and parsed once, when the counter
style is compiled against the built language
(`compile`) into a `CounterStyle`. It also
holds three choices about links and ranges, and may ask for a number writer
other than the default one. The concepts overview presents counters and
counter styles together (counters and counter
styles).

A feature contributes the declaration to the service slot
`STYLES_SLOT`; a counter refers to its default counter
style by name (`CounterDecl::default_style`),
and a reference point gives the counter style of its number in its number
source. A host replaces a declared counter style by name through
`NumberingConfig`.

A counter style's name is a dotted name owned by the feature that declares
it, such as `flm.math.style.equation`, so that two features may each
declare a counter style for the same counter without a clash.

oneOf.description:
A number template in the template language: every `#{name}` is the
number written in the format `name`, and the rest is written as given:
`#{arabic}.` writes `3.` for the number three, and
`\textbf{#{arabic}}` writes it in bold. A `#{…}` whose name is not a
number format is refused when the counter style is compiled, and so is
a key in brackets, `#[…]{…}`, which only a within template accepts.

A number template in the single-letter language: the first character
among `a`, `A`, `i`, `I` and `1` is the number, written in the format
that character shows by example (letters, capital letters, roman
numerals, capital roman numerals, decimal digits), and the rest is
FLM written as given: `(a)` writes `(c)` for the number three. A text
that holds none of those five characters writes itself for every
number, and the parts of the counters it is numbered within are not
written before it: it is a fixed mark, such as a bullet.

This is the language of an author's own item labels, where the
number's format is shown by an example instead of being named. The
first of the five characters is replaced wherever it is, so `Part a.`
writes `Pcrt a.` for the number three; a text that must hold one of
these characters as a letter of its own is written in the `Formats`
language.

NumberTemplate.description:
A number template: how a counter style writes the number itself, as a text
with a place for the number, written in one of the eight `NumberFormat`s;
a counter style holds one in its field `number_format`.

The text is FLM with a place for the number, in one of two languages, and
it is compiled once, when the counter style is compiled. Around the place
for the number the text is ordinary FLM: `\textbf` and `~` mean in a
number template what they mean in a document.

- `Formats` is written in the template language
  that user definitions use (the template language shared by
  features):
  `#{name}` is the number written in the format `name`. The whole text is
  parsed as one, so markup may surround the number: `\textbf{#{arabic}}`
  writes the number in bold.
- `Initial` is the language of an author's own
  item labels: the first of the characters `a`, `A`, `i`, `I` and `1` is
  the number, written in the format that character shows by example, and
  the rest is FLM: `(a)` writes `(c)` for the number three.

A counter style's number format
(`CounterStyleDecl::number_format`),
each of its sub-levels (`SubLevelDecl`) and a
reference point's own number template
(`NumberSource::number_format`,
always in the `Formats` language) are number templates.

separator.description:
The text written before this level's number, when something is
written before it.

number_format.description: How this level's number is written.

SubLevelDecl.description:
A sub-level of a counter style: how the sub-numbers at one level are
written, and the separator written before each.

A counter style with one sub-level, declared as letters after a full stop,
writes the value `(3, 2)` as `3.b`. The separator is FLM; it is left out
when nothing has been written before the sub-number, so that the end of a
range is written `b` and not `.b`.

base.description:
The words used when no variant is asked for, and when the variant asked
for is not declared.

PrefixWords.description:
The prefix words of a counter style: the words written before a number by
default, and the named variants that a request may ask for instead.

A variant is a complete pair of words under a name of its own, such as
`capital`, holding `Equation~` and `Equations~` where the default words are
`Eq.~` and `Eqs.~`. A request for a variant the counter style does not
declare (`FormatOptions::variant`) gets the default words; the refs
feature reports such a request at the reference as an Error.

one.description: The word written before a single number.

other.description: The word written before several numbers.

PluralWords.description:
The word written before a number, in two forms: one for a single number
and one for several.

The fields are named after the plural categories `one` and `other` of
natural-language pluralization: `Eq.~` for one equation, `Eqs.~` for
several. Both are FLM, so `~` and a text style mean in them what they mean
in a document.

open.description: The text written before the number.

close.description: The text written after the number.

Delimiters.description:
The delimiters of a counter style: the text before and the text after a
number, such as `(` and `)` for an equation number shown as `(3)`.

Both are FLM, and both are left out when a number is asked for without
delimiters (`FormatOptions::without_delimiters`).

one_pre.description: Before a single run. Default: empty.

one_post.description: After a single run. Default: empty.

range_pre.description: Before a run of several numbers. Default: empty.

range_mid.description: Between the ends of a run of three or more. Default: `${endash}`.

range_pairmid.description:
Between the ends of a run of exactly two. Default: `${sep}`; compact:
`,`.

range_post.description: After a run of several numbers. Default: empty.

list_pre.description: Before three runs or more. Default: empty.

list_mid.description:
Between the runs of a list, except before the last. Default: `${sep} `;
compact: `,`.

list_midlast.description: Before the last run of a list. Default: `${sep} ${and} `; compact: `,`.

list_post.description: After three runs or more. Default: empty.

empty.description:
The text written when there is no number at all, and the variable
`empty`. Default: `(empty)`.

JoinDecl.description:
The join texts of a counter style: the texts that join several numbers
into one text, such as `1–3, 7, and 9`.

Every field is a text written between or around the numbers, and each may
be left unset, in which case the default text is used (the defaults are
given per field below). The texts are FLM. A `${name}` in one of them is
replaced by the text of the key `name`, in one pass (a replaced text is not
scanned again); the keys meant for this use are the four variables `and`,
`sep`, `endash` and `empty`, so that a caller changes the word `and` once
instead of in every join text that uses it. A `${name}` whose name is not a key fails the
compilation of the counter style (`StyleError::UnknownVariable`).

Which fields are used depends on how many *runs* the numbers form, a run
being one number or a sequence of consecutive numbers:

- one run: `one_pre`, the run, `one_post`;
- two runs: `pair_pre`, the first, `pair_mid`, the second, `pair_post`;
- more: `list_pre`, the runs separated by `list_mid`, `list_midlast`
  before the last one, `list_post`.

A run of several numbers is written as `range_pre`, the first number, then
`range_pairmid` for a run of exactly two or `range_mid` for a longer one,
then the last number, then `range_post`.

The refs feature uses the same declaration for the texts that join the
targets of a reference to several targets.

counters.description: What the document says about each counter it mentions, in name order.

NumberingOptions.description:
The numbering options of a document: per counter, the counter within which
it is numbered, and the value it has before it is first advanced.

These are the per-document option values of the numbering feature: an
option type bound on the document, which a render request may set again,
its value then replacing the document's for that render
(`Bind::Either`). In data, they are
the settings key `counters` of the numbering feature, a map from a
counter's name to its `CounterOptions`.

Whether a reference point is numbered at all is not an option of this
feature: a point whose number source gives a counter is numbered, and the
feature that owns the point decides whether it gives one (for example the
numbering depth of the headings feature, fixed when the registry is built).

A counter that the options do not mention keeps what its declaring feature
said. The numbering stage reports, once per run, every entry it cannot
apply, and applies the others:

- an entry for a counter no feature declares is a Warning
  (`flm.numbering.unknown-counter`) and changes nothing; an entry that
  numbers a counter within a counter no feature declares is the same
  Warning, and its `within` changes nothing (its `initial` still applies);
- an entry that numbers a counter within a parent set no feature registers
  (`flm.numbering.unknown-parent-set`), within no counter at all (an empty
  list of parents, or a parent set that holds no counter;
  `flm.numbering.bad-within-joiner`), or through a within-joiner that does
  not compile (`flm.numbering.bad-within-joiner`) or that no feature
  registers (`flm.numbering.unknown-within-joiner`), is an Error, and its
  `within` changes nothing (its `initial` still applies);
- an entry whose within-joiner writes a counter that, under the options,
  is not always one of the counters the counter is numbered within is an
  Error (`flm.numbering.not-an-ancestor`), and the counter keeps the place
  it was declared with;
- an entry that moves a counter's ancestors so that the declared
  within-joiner or nesting joiner of a counter writes a counter it is no
  longer always numbered within is an Error
  (`flm.numbering.not-an-ancestor`), and no point counting in that counter
  is numbered in that run;
- entries that make counters numbered within each other are an Error
  (`flm.numbering.hierarchy-cycle`), and no point counting in those
  counters is numbered in that run.

within.description:
The counter's place in the hierarchy of counters. `None` keeps the
place its declaration gives.

initial.description:
The value the counter has before it is first advanced, or `None` for a
counter that has no value until then.

A counter with no value cannot be written, so a reference point
numbered within it takes no number and is reported as the Error
`flm.numbering.parent-uninitialized`. `Some(0)` gives the counter the
value `0`, so that a subsection written before any section is numbered
`0.1`. The counter is then advanced from that value: `Some(3)` makes
the first section `4`. The value applies under every combination of
the values of the counter's ancestors: an initial `0` for
`flm.headings.subsection` makes a subsubsection written in a section
that has no subsection yet read as though the subsection had the value
0, `1.0.1`. When the parent that applies is chosen among several, the
counters with initial values count as advanced before the document
begins, the outermost counter first.

CounterOptions.description:
What a document's numbering options say about one counter: the counter
within which it is numbered, and the value it has before it is first
advanced. A field left `None` keeps what the counter was declared with.

oneOf.description:
Numbered within nothing: nothing restarts the counter, and no other
counter's number is written before its number.

A document uses it to take a counter out of a hierarchy it does not
want. For example, a document whose subsections come before any
section, or whose sections are never advanced, numbers its subsections
within nothing, or gives the sections an
`initial` value.

Numbered within the counters this `Within` gives, with the numbers
written by its within-joiner.

WithinOption.description:
The place in the hierarchy of counters that a document's numbering options
give a counter, replacing the place the declaring feature gave it.

The place decides two things: what restarts the counter, and what is
written before its number.

parents.description:
The counter within which this counter is numbered, or the counters any
one of which may be its parent. The parent that applies restarts this
counter: the counter's count is kept separately for each list of
ancestors it is advanced under, each ancestor identified by its name
and its value.

joiner.description:
The within-joiner: how the ancestors' numbers are written before this
counter's own.

no_restart.description:
Whether the parent is left out of what restarts the count. `true`
continues the count across the parent's advances, and the parent's
number is still written before the counter's own (`1.1`, `1.2`,
`2.3`). `false` by default.

Within.description:
The counter within which a counter is numbered, and how that counter's
number is written before the counter's own: the counter's place in the
hierarchy of counters.

A subsection numbered within a section is written `2.3`: the parent is the
counter `flm.headings.section`, and the within-joiner is the joining text
`.`. The two are declared together because the parent decides what
restarts the counter and the within-joiner decides what is shown of the
parent, and neither is of any use without the other. The module
documentation describes the
mechanism.

Three constructors say which counter is the parent:

- `Within::parent`: numbered within that one counter.
- `Within::parents`: numbered within whichever of several counters was
  advanced most recently in document order.
- `Within::parent_set`: the same over the counters of a parent set that
  a feature registered (`ParentSetDecl`).

Each writes the parent's number and a full stop before the counter's own
number, `1.2`. Four builders change what is written:

- `joined_by`: another joining text.
- `template`: a within template, which may write
  markup around an ancestor's number and may refer to more than one
  ancestor.
- `displayed_bare`: nothing of the parent is
  written; the counter restarts under the parent and its number is shown
  bare.
- `joiner_named`: a within-joiner that a feature
  registered by name, which writes what its code writes.

The builder `no_restart` keeps the parent's number
written before the counter's own but stops the parent from restarting the
count: `1.1`, `1.2`, `2.3`.

oneOf.description: Numbered within this one counter.

Numbered within whichever of these counters was advanced most
recently.

Numbered within whichever counter of the parent set of this name was
advanced most recently. A name no feature registers fails the registry
build when a feature declares it, and is the Error
`flm.numbering.unknown-parent-set` when a document's numbering options
give it.

Parents.description:
Which counters a counter may be numbered within: one counter, any counter
of a list, or any counter of a registered parent set.

This is the `parents` field of `Within`, which the constructors
`Within::parent`, `Within::parents` and `Within::parent_set` set.

Where there are several possible parents, the **parent that applies** at a
reference point is the one among them that was advanced most recently in
document order. For example, an equation numbered within any of the
sectioning counters is written `4.1` after a chapter and before the
chapter's first section, and `4.1.2` once a section has begun in that
chapter.

oneOf.description:
The parent's number, then this joining text, which is FLM: what
`Within::parent` and `Within::joined_by` make. A subsection joined
by `.` is written `1.2`.

The parent is written with its own ancestors before it, each as a part
of its own, so a chain three counters deep is written `1.2.3` with
every counter declaring only its joining text.

A within template, in the language that `Within::template`
describes.

Nothing of the ancestors is written: the counter restarts under its
parent, and its number is shown **bare**, that is, without its
parents' numbers. What `Within::displayed_bare` makes.

The within-joiner registered under this name in
`WITHIN_JOINERS_SLOT`, which writes what its code writes. A name no
feature registers is refused: in a feature's declaration it fails the
registry build, and in a document's numbering options it is the Error
`flm.numbering.unknown-within-joiner`, and the counter keeps the
hierarchy it was declared with.

WithinJoinerSpec.description:
The form of a within-joiner, which writes a counter's ancestors' numbers
before the counter's own number: one of the four forms a `Within` may
carry.

A form is data, not behavior: it can be compared, hashed, and carried in a
document's numbering options. What a form writes is decided when it is
compiled, against the built language and against the within-joiners the
registry holds (`Within::compile`).

math.description:
Whether the lines of `equation`, `align` and `gather` are numbered (`true` by default). Fixed when the registry is built: it cannot vary per document or per render.

How the recomposed LaTeX writes a display-math environment: the LaTeX written before and after it, and whether the environment is written through the command `\flmMathEnvironment`. Set per render request.

numbered_equations.description:
Whether the lines of `equation`, `align` and `gather` that carry no
`\nonumber` and no `\tag` are numbered. `true` by default. The lines
of `equation*`, `align*` and `gather*` are never numbered.

surround_display_math.description:
The LaTeX written, byte for byte, before and after every displayed
formula: every display-math environment and every displayed math group
(`\[…\]`). Both empty by default.

emit_flm_math_environment_macro.description:
Whether an environment is written as
`\flmMathEnvironment{<name>}{<arguments>}{<body>}` rather than as
`\begin{<name>}…\end{<name>}`. Off by default. The style file then
holds the definition of `\flmMathEnvironment`, which a user may
redefine.

numbered_equations.description:
Whether the lines of `equation`, `align` and `gather` that carry no
`\nonumber` and no `\tag` are numbered. `true` by default. The lines
of `equation*`, `align*` and `gather*` are never numbered.

MathConfig.description:
The configuration of the `math` feature: whether the lines of the
unstarred display-math environments are numbered.

A feature's configuration is the plain Rust value the feature is
constructed from; it is fixed when the registry is built (settings,
options and
configuration).
This setting must be fixed when the registry is built, because the
reference points that an environment declares depend on it, and the code
that declares them (the element's `Referenceable` aspect; see elements
and aspects) cannot
read an option set per document or per render. The feature adds
`digest_bytes` to the registry digest, so that
two registries built with different configurations have different
digests.

surround_display_math.description:
The LaTeX written, byte for byte, before and after every displayed
formula: every display-math environment and every displayed math group
(`\[…\]`). Both empty by default.

emit_flm_math_environment_macro.description:
Whether an environment is written as
`\flmMathEnvironment{<name>}{<arguments>}{<body>}` rather than as
`\begin{<name>}…\end{<name>}`. Off by default. The style file then
holds the definition of `\flmMathEnvironment`, which a user may
redefine.

MathRecomposeOptions.description:
The options of the `math` feature that say how the recomposed LaTeX writes a
displayed formula: an option type (`crate::model::options`) whose
values are set on a render request
(`Bind::Render`). The rules of a
feature that processes mathematics read them on the `latex-recomposed`
backend, through the parts of this module (see the module documentation).

refs.description:
The texts that join the items of a reference to several targets. Fixed when the registry is built: it cannot vary per document or per render.

Whether a reference that points at no label is reported as an Error (the default) or, under `unresolved: allow`, as a Warning. Set per render request.

How the recomposed LaTeX writes labels and references: the label types written as the document wrote them instead of as generated keys, and whether a reference is protected against a command that changes the case of its argument. Set per render request.

join.description:
The texts that join the items of a reference to several targets.
Default: the defaults of `JoinDecl`.

unresolved.description:
The severity of a reference that points at no label: `error` (the
default) or `allow` (a Warning).

safe_label_types.description:
Per label type (`sec`, `eq`), how its labels are written; a type not
listed is `Safe`. Empty by default. A label
with no type belongs to none of these and is always written by its
safe label.

**You own this: a type set to `Raw`.** Its labels
are written as the document spelled them instead of as a generated
safe label. You must ensure that those labels are spellings LaTeX can
carry through its auxiliary file: a label holding a character LaTeX
treats specially cannot be read back, which the safe labels exist to
avoid.

protect.description:
Whether a reference is wrapped in `\NoCaseChange{\protect …}`, which
keeps it out of a command that changes the case of its argument
(`\MakeUppercase`). Off by default; when on, the style file requests
the `textcase` package, which supplies `\NoCaseChange` on every LaTeX
kernel.

A reference left unwrapped inside such a command is uppercased whole,
its options and its safe label alike, and it fails in two ways,
neither of which raises an error.
`\MakeUppercase{… \flmRef[noprefix]{ref1} …}` passes the hook
`NOPREFIX`, a key it does not translate, so it is dropped and the name
the author left out comes back. And the safe label itself is
uppercased, so LaTeX looks for a label `REF1`, finds none, and prints
`??` with only a warning. Turn this on for a document whose headings
or captions are uppercased.

join.description:
The texts that join the items of a reference to several targets.
Default: the defaults of `JoinDecl`.

RefsConfig.description:
The configuration of the `refs` feature: the texts that join the
items of a reference to several targets.

A `\ref` with several targets is written as one list. Its first items are
the numbers of the targets the document numbered, one item per counter
style, each written by that style, the styles in the order the reference
first reaches them; then comes each target without a number, in the order
the reference wrote them. `join` joins the items. It is
a `JoinDecl`, the type a counter style declares its own joining texts
with, with the same keys, the same variables `${and}` and `${sep}` and the
same defaults, so that a caller changes the word "and" the same way in both
places. By default, two items read `Eq. (1) and Thm. 1.1`, and three read
`Eq. (1), Thm. 1.1, and A note`.

One item is written `one_pre`, the item, `one_post`. Two items are written
`pair_pre`, the first, `pair_mid`, the second, `pair_post`. Three or more
are written `list_pre`, the items with `list_mid` between them and
`list_midlast` before the last, then `list_post`. The range texts
(`range_pre`, `range_mid`, `range_pairmid`, `range_post`) and the `empty`
text never apply to a reference list, whose items are never ranges of
several items; they are still accepted, so that one `JoinDecl` can serve
a counter style and this list.

A feature's configuration is the plain Rust value the feature is
constructed from; it is fixed when the registry is built (settings,
options and
configuration).
Every text is parsed as FLM once, when the registry is built: a text that
does not parse, or that refers to a variable nothing defines, fails the
registry build, as a counter style's text does. Because the configuration
changes what the registry produces, the feature adds
`digest_bytes` to the registry digest.

one_pre.description: Before a single run. Default: empty.

one_post.description: After a single run. Default: empty.

range_pre.description: Before a run of several numbers. Default: empty.

range_mid.description: Between the ends of a run of three or more. Default: `${endash}`.

range_pairmid.description:
Between the ends of a run of exactly two. Default: `${sep}`; compact:
`,`.

range_post.description: After a run of several numbers. Default: empty.

list_pre.description: Before three runs or more. Default: empty.

list_mid.description:
Between the runs of a list, except before the last. Default: `${sep} `;
compact: `,`.

list_midlast.description: Before the last run of a list. Default: `${sep} ${and} `; compact: `,`.

list_post.description: After three runs or more. Default: empty.

empty.description:
The text written when there is no number at all, and the variable
`empty`. Default: `(empty)`.

JoinDecl.description:
The join texts of a counter style: the texts that join several numbers
into one text, such as `1–3, 7, and 9`.

Every field is a text written between or around the numbers, and each may
be left unset, in which case the default text is used (the defaults are
given per field below). The texts are FLM. A `${name}` in one of them is
replaced by the text of the key `name`, in one pass (a replaced text is not
scanned again); the keys meant for this use are the four variables `and`,
`sep`, `endash` and `empty`, so that a caller changes the word `and` once
instead of in every join text that uses it. A `${name}` whose name is not a key fails the
compilation of the counter style (`StyleError::UnknownVariable`).

Which fields are used depends on how many *runs* the numbers form, a run
being one number or a sequence of consecutive numbers:

- one run: `one_pre`, the run, `one_post`;
- two runs: `pair_pre`, the first, `pair_mid`, the second, `pair_post`;
- more: `list_pre`, the runs separated by `list_mid`, `list_midlast`
  before the last one, `list_post`.

A run of several numbers is written as `range_pre`, the first number, then
`range_pairmid` for a run of exactly two or `range_mid` for a longer one,
then the last number, then `range_post`.

The refs feature uses the same declaration for the texts that join the
targets of a reference to several targets.

unresolved.description:
The severity of a reference that points at no label: `error` (the
default) or `allow` (a Warning).

RefsRenderOptions.description:
The render options of the `refs` feature, an option type
(`crate::model::options`) set per render request.

In a plan that renders nothing, such as one of the `check` workflow, an
unresolved reference is always a Warning, and these options do not apply;
see the module documentation.

oneOf.description:
An Error diagnostic. A run that has recorded an Error stops before it
writes its outputs, unless the caller lets it continue
(`RunOptions`).

A Warning diagnostic: the output is written, and the reference shows
its label text, marked unresolved.

UnresolvedRefs.description:
The severity of a reference that points at no label. The value is set per
render request, as part of `RefsRenderOptions`.

safe_label_types.description:
Per label type (`sec`, `eq`), how its labels are written; a type not
listed is `Safe`. Empty by default. A label
with no type belongs to none of these and is always written by its
safe label.

**You own this: a type set to `Raw`.** Its labels
are written as the document spelled them instead of as a generated
safe label. You must ensure that those labels are spellings LaTeX can
carry through its auxiliary file: a label holding a character LaTeX
treats specially cannot be read back, which the safe labels exist to
avoid.

protect.description:
Whether a reference is wrapped in `\NoCaseChange{\protect …}`, which
keeps it out of a command that changes the case of its argument
(`\MakeUppercase`). Off by default; when on, the style file requests
the `textcase` package, which supplies `\NoCaseChange` on every LaTeX
kernel.

A reference left unwrapped inside such a command is uppercased whole,
its options and its safe label alike, and it fails in two ways,
neither of which raises an error.
`\MakeUppercase{… \flmRef[noprefix]{ref1} …}` passes the hook
`NOPREFIX`, a key it does not translate, so it is dropped and the name
the author left out comes back. And the safe label itself is
uppercased, so LaTeX looks for a label `REF1`, finds none, and prints
`??` with only a warning. Turn this on for a document whose headings
or captions are uppercased.

RefsRecomposeOptions.description:
The render options of the `refs` feature's recomposition rules: how the
recomposed LaTeX writes labels and references (see the module
documentation). An option type (`crate::model::options`) declared with
`Bind::Render`: its value is set per
render request.

oneOf.description: The safe label allocated for the label (`ref3`). The default.

The label as the document wrote it (`sec:intro`), byte for byte; no
safe label is allocated for it.

SafeLabelMode.description:
How the recomposed LaTeX writes the labels of one label type: by their
safe label, or as the document wrote them.

headings.description:
The heading kinds and the heading commands that write them: each kind's level, counter, counter style, the counter it is numbered within, number format, heading title template, table-of-contents and run-in settings and reference point; each command's heading kind and default options; and which kinds are numbered. Fixed when the registry is built: it cannot vary per document or per render.

The LaTeX sectioning command each heading kind is written as in the recomposed LaTeX, keyed by the kind's name; a kind not listed is written as the command of its own name. Set per render request.
The heading kinds, in the order they were given.

commands.description: The heading commands, in the order they were given.

numbering.description:
Which kinds are numbered: `HeadingNumbering::NothingNumbered` by
default.

latex_commands.description:
The LaTeX sectioning command, without the backslash, that each heading
kind is written as, keyed by the kind's name. A kind the map does not list
is written as the command of its own name. Empty by default.

headings.description: The heading kinds, in the order they were given.

commands.description: The heading commands, in the order they were given.

numbering.description:
Which kinds are numbered: `HeadingNumbering::NothingNumbered` by
default.

HeadingsConfig.description:
The configuration of the `headings` feature: the heading kinds the
registry declares, the heading commands that write them, and which kinds are
numbered.

`HeadingsConfig::new` is the standard configuration: the five kinds
`section`, `subsection`, `subsubsection`, `paragraph` and `subparagraph`, at
levels 1 to 5, each counting in the counter `flm.headings.<kind>`, the first
three written in decimal digits and the last two in letters. Each kind except
`section` is numbered within the kind above it, except `paragraph`, which is
numbered within whichever of `section`, `subsection` and `subsubsection` came
last and is shown without their numbers. There is one command per kind, with
the kind's own name and no defaults, and no kind is numbered
(`numbering`).

`Headings::new` takes this value, and a program passes it through
`StdcoreConfig::headings`. A
feature's configuration is fixed when the registry is built (see settings,
options and
configuration).
This configuration must be fixed then, because the commands the language accepts
and the block structure a run freezes depend on it. For the same reason the
feature adds `digest_bytes` to the registry digest
(`crate::model::digest`), the fingerprint that decides whether a cached result may be reused.

The feature checks the configuration when it registers
(`HeadingsConfig::validate`). Each of these fails the registry build with an
error that says what clashed: two kinds with one name, two commands with one
name, a command that writes a kind no declaration has, two kinds with one
counter or one counter style, a kind with a counter and no counter style, and
a command default whose key is not `numbered` or `toc`, or whose value is not
`true` or `false`. A kind that no command writes is accepted: its element
value is registered as synthesized, with no name, and a program may create
its headings itself, for instance in a stage.

level.description:
The level, a number counted from zero, smaller for outer headings: the
level the `Sectioning` aspect returns, which, unless a render option maps the
kind to a tag, chooses the HTML tag, and which chooses how
the plain-text backend prints the heading. Every value is a level; the
standard kinds have levels 1 to 5, and level 0 is available for a kind
declared above the sections, such as a chapter.

counter.description:
The counter the kind's headings count in, or `None` for a kind that is
never numbered, which declares nothing to the `numbering` feature.
`flm.headings.<name>` by default (`COUNTER_PREFIX`).

style.description:
The counter style the kind's numbers are shown in:
`flm.headings.style.<name>` by default (`STYLE_PREFIX`). A kind with
a counter needs one; `HeadingDecl::no_counter` clears both.

within.description:
The counter the kind's counter is numbered within, and how that
counter's number is written before the kind's own; `None`, the default,
for a counter numbered within nothing. It refers to counters by their
full names: `Within::parent("flm.headings.section")`.

number_format.description:
How the kind's own number is written, in the number-template language
of `NumberTemplate`: `#{arabic}` by default.

title_number_format.description:
The kind's heading title template: what is written before the title of
a numbered heading of the kind. It is a text in the template language
(see the template language shared by
features)
in which `#{number}` is the heading's number; `DEFAULT_TITLE_NUMBER_FORMAT`
(`#{number}. `) by default, so a numbered section reads `1. Introduction`.

It states how the number joins the title (the text around it, which may
hold a word: `Chapter~#{number}: `), and not how the number looks, which
a program's lowering rule or a stylesheet decides through the role
`NUMBER_ROLE` the number carries.
`#[bare]{number}` writes the kind's own number without the numbers of
its parent counters, and `#[Roman]{number}` writes it in another number
format; markup may enclose the placeholder. A template without any
placeholder is allowed: the heading then shows nothing of its number and
still counts. Nothing is written for a heading that is not numbered. A
template that does not parse, that uses another placeholder, or that
gives `number` a key it does not take, fails the registry build with an
error that gives the kind. See `title` for the full description.

skip_toc.description:
Whether the kind is never listed in a table of contents, regardless of
what a heading writes for `toc`. `false` by default.

run_in.description:
Whether the kind is set as a run-in heading, at the start of the
paragraph it introduces. `false` by default.

ref_kind.description: The reference kind of the kind's reference point: `KIND` by default.

label_types.description:
The label types the kind's reference point accepts: `LABEL_TYPES` by
default.

anchor_prefix.description:
The text that begins the anchor of a heading without a label:
`ANCHOR_PREFIX` by default.

docs.description:
What the kind is, in one sentence, for the description of its element
value in the registry. Empty by default; an empty text is replaced there
by `A heading of level <level>.`, with the kind's level.

HeadingDecl.description:
The declaration of one heading kind: what a heading is (a section, a
subsection, an appendix), declared by name with its level and everything a
heading of the kind needs.

`HeadingDecl::new` fills in every field except the name and the level with
the defaults of the standard kinds; one builder method per field changes it. The
kinds a registry has are `HeadingsConfig::headings`, and the commands that
write a kind are `HeadingsConfig::commands`: a heading kind's declaration
lists no command, because several commands may write one kind.

parents.description:
The counter within which this counter is numbered, or the counters any
one of which may be its parent. The parent that applies restarts this
counter: the counter's count is kept separately for each list of
ancestors it is advanced under, each ancestor identified by its name
and its value.

joiner.description:
The within-joiner: how the ancestors' numbers are written before this
counter's own.

no_restart.description:
Whether the parent is left out of what restarts the count. `true`
continues the count across the parent's advances, and the parent's
number is still written before the counter's own (`1.1`, `1.2`,
`2.3`). `false` by default.

Within.description:
The counter within which a counter is numbered, and how that counter's
number is written before the counter's own: the counter's place in the
hierarchy of counters.

A subsection numbered within a section is written `2.3`: the parent is the
counter `flm.headings.section`, and the within-joiner is the joining text
`.`. The two are declared together because the parent decides what
restarts the counter and the within-joiner decides what is shown of the
parent, and neither is of any use without the other. The module
documentation describes the
mechanism.

Three constructors say which counter is the parent:

- `Within::parent`: numbered within that one counter.
- `Within::parents`: numbered within whichever of several counters was
  advanced most recently in document order.
- `Within::parent_set`: the same over the counters of a parent set that
  a feature registered (`ParentSetDecl`).

Each writes the parent's number and a full stop before the counter's own
number, `1.2`. Four builders change what is written:

- `joined_by`: another joining text.
- `template`: a within template, which may write
  markup around an ancestor's number and may refer to more than one
  ancestor.
- `displayed_bare`: nothing of the parent is
  written; the counter restarts under the parent and its number is shown
  bare.
- `joiner_named`: a within-joiner that a feature
  registered by name, which writes what its code writes.

The builder `no_restart` keeps the parent's number
written before the counter's own but stops the parent from restarting the
count: `1.1`, `1.2`, `2.3`.

oneOf.description: Numbered within this one counter.

Numbered within whichever of these counters was advanced most
recently.

Numbered within whichever counter of the parent set of this name was
advanced most recently. A name no feature registers fails the registry
build when a feature declares it, and is the Error
`flm.numbering.unknown-parent-set` when a document's numbering options
give it.

Parents.description:
Which counters a counter may be numbered within: one counter, any counter
of a list, or any counter of a registered parent set.

This is the `parents` field of `Within`, which the constructors
`Within::parent`, `Within::parents` and `Within::parent_set` set.

Where there are several possible parents, the **parent that applies** at a
reference point is the one among them that was advanced most recently in
document order. For example, an equation numbered within any of the
sectioning counters is written `4.1` after a chapter and before the
chapter's first section, and `4.1.2` once a section has begun in that
chapter.

oneOf.description:
The parent's number, then this joining text, which is FLM: what
`Within::parent` and `Within::joined_by` make. A subsection joined
by `.` is written `1.2`.

The parent is written with its own ancestors before it, each as a part
of its own, so a chain three counters deep is written `1.2.3` with
every counter declaring only its joining text.

A within template, in the language that `Within::template`
describes.

Nothing of the ancestors is written: the counter restarts under its
parent, and its number is shown **bare**, that is, without its
parents' numbers. What `Within::displayed_bare` makes.

The within-joiner registered under this name in
`WITHIN_JOINERS_SLOT`, which writes what its code writes. A name no
feature registers is refused: in a feature's declaration it fails the
registry build, and in a document's numbering options it is the Error
`flm.numbering.unknown-within-joiner`, and the counter keeps the
hierarchy it was declared with.

WithinJoinerSpec.description:
The form of a within-joiner, which writes a counter's ancestors' numbers
before the counter's own number: one of the four forms a `Within` may
carry.

A form is data, not behavior: it can be compared, hashed, and carried in a
document's numbering options. What a form writes is decided when it is
compiled, against the built language and against the within-joiners the
registry holds (`Within::compile`).

oneOf.description:
A number template in the template language: every `#{name}` is the
number written in the format `name`, and the rest is written as given:
`#{arabic}.` writes `3.` for the number three, and
`\textbf{#{arabic}}` writes it in bold. A `#{…}` whose name is not a
number format is refused when the counter style is compiled, and so is
a key in brackets, `#[…]{…}`, which only a within template accepts.

A number template in the single-letter language: the first character
among `a`, `A`, `i`, `I` and `1` is the number, written in the format
that character shows by example (letters, capital letters, roman
numerals, capital roman numerals, decimal digits), and the rest is
FLM written as given: `(a)` writes `(c)` for the number three. A text
that holds none of those five characters writes itself for every
number, and the parts of the counters it is numbered within are not
written before it: it is a fixed mark, such as a bullet.

This is the language of an author's own item labels, where the
number's format is shown by an example instead of being named. The
first of the five characters is replaced wherever it is, so `Part a.`
writes `Pcrt a.` for the number three; a text that must hold one of
these characters as a letter of its own is written in the `Formats`
language.

NumberTemplate.description:
A number template: how a counter style writes the number itself, as a text
with a place for the number, written in one of the eight `NumberFormat`s;
a counter style holds one in its field `number_format`.

The text is FLM with a place for the number, in one of two languages, and
it is compiled once, when the counter style is compiled. Around the place
for the number the text is ordinary FLM: `\textbf` and `~` mean in a
number template what they mean in a document.

- `Formats` is written in the template language
  that user definitions use (the template language shared by
  features):
  `#{name}` is the number written in the format `name`. The whole text is
  parsed as one, so markup may surround the number: `\textbf{#{arabic}}`
  writes the number in bold.
- `Initial` is the language of an author's own
  item labels: the first of the characters `a`, `A`, `i`, `I` and `1` is
  the number, written in the format that character shows by example, and
  the rest is FLM: `(a)` writes `(c)` for the number three.

A counter style's number format
(`CounterStyleDecl::number_format`),
each of its sub-levels (`SubLevelDecl`) and a
reference point's own number template
(`NumberSource::number_format`,
always in the `Formats` language) are number templates.

heading.description: The name of the heading kind it writes.

defaults.description:
The options a heading written with this command has before its star and
its bracket are read, as key-value pairs in the order they are read.

HeadingCommand.description:
The declaration of one heading command: a macro an author writes, such as
`\section`, the heading kind it writes, and the options a heading written
with it has before the heading's own star and bracket are read.

Several commands may write one kind. Every command takes the same
arguments (`heading_args`); two commands of one kind differ only by their
defaults, which are read before the star and the bracket and are replaced by
them (see the module
documentation).
A default's key is `NUMBERED_KEY` or `TOC_KEY` and its value `true` or
`false`; any other default fails the registry build.

oneOf.description: No kind is numbered. The default.
Every kind that has a counter is numbered.

Every kind that has a counter and whose level is this number or less
is numbered: `UpToDepth(2)` numbers the sections and the subsections of
the standard kinds.

HeadingNumbering.description:
Which heading kinds are numbered: the numbering depth of a `HeadingsConfig`.

A kind is numbered when it has a counter and the depth admits its level.
The depth is fixed when the registry is built; a heading of a numbered kind
may still opt out with a star or `numbered=false`.

latex_commands.description:
The LaTeX sectioning command, without the backslash, that each heading
kind is written as, keyed by the kind's name. A kind the map does not list
is written as the command of its own name. Empty by default.

HeadingsLatexOptions.description:
The render options of the headings on the recomposed LaTeX: which LaTeX
sectioning command each heading kind is written as.

The option type is declared with
`Bind::Render`, so its value is set on
the render request and is part of the plan key
(`PlanKey`), the digest under which a built plan can
be cached. The feature declares it
whether or not the registry holds the `latex-recomposed` backend; only
`LATEX_RULE` reads it. In settings data, its key is `latex_commands`.

lists.description: The list environments: for each list kind, its environment name, whether its items are numbered, its label templates and its reference templates (read for a numbered list kind) by nesting depth, and its nesting joiner. Fixed when the registry is built: it cannot vary per document or per render.

environments.description: The list kinds, by environment name.
The list kinds, by environment name.

ListsConfig.description:
The configuration of the `Lists` feature: the list
environments, each environment's name mapped to its list kind
(`ListKind`).

The default (`ListsConfig::new`) declares three list kinds:

| environment | numbered | labels by depth | reference templates by depth |
|---|---|---|---|
| `itemize` | no | `•`, `-`, `▸` | ignored: a reference shows the label |
| `enumerate` | yes | `#{arabic}.`, `(#{roman})`, `#{alph}-` | `#{arabic}`, `(#{roman})`, `#{alph}` |
| `description` | no | none: every item carries its term as a tag | ignored: a reference shows the tag |

An `enumerate` therefore shows `1.`, `2.` beside its items, a list
nested in one of its items `(i)`, `(ii)`, and a list nested one level
deeper `a-`, `b-`, while references to those items show `Item~2`,
`Item~(ii)`, `Item~b`. A program that embeds the library declares other
list kinds, or changes these, through the same type:

`Lists::new` takes the value, and the standard
package carries it as
`StdcoreConfig::lists`. It is the
feature's configuration (see
configuration):
fixed when the registry is built, before any document is parsed, because
the environments are part of the parsing language the registry builds
(`BuiltLang`) and the counters and counter
styles the feature declares depend on it. The feature therefore feeds
`digest_bytes` into the registry digest, the
fingerprint that decides whether a cached result may be reused, as every
feature whose declarations depend on its configuration must.

The registry build checks the configuration and fails on:

- an environment name that is empty or holds whitespace, a brace, a
  backslash or a `%` (`ListsConfig::validate`);
- an environment name that is one of the kind tokens a presentation list
  reserves (`LIST_RESERVED_KINDS`; `validate`);
- a numbered list kind with no label template or no reference template
  (`validate`);
- once the parsing language is built, a label template, or a numbered list kind's
  reference template, that is not valid in the template language, and a
  label template of an unnumbered list kind that writes a number format.

numbered.description: Whether the items of a list of this list kind are numbered.

labels.description:
The label templates by nesting depth, the outermost first; the last
one serves every deeper list. An empty vector means that no label is
shown unless the author writes one: every item must then carry a tag,
as in a `description` list. A numbered list kind has at least one.

ref_labels.description:
The reference templates by nesting depth, the outermost first; the
last one serves every deeper list. For a numbered list kind, each is
the number format of the counter style of its depth: it is what a
reference to an item shows (`Item~1`) and what the nesting joiner
writes of an enclosing item. A numbered list kind has at least one.
For an unnumbered list kind they are ignored: its items have no
number, and a reference to one of them shows its label.

nesting.description:
For a numbered list kind, what an item of a nested list of this list
kind writes of the enclosing item's number; unused for an unnumbered
one. `WithinJoinerSpec::Bare`, which writes nothing, by default.

ListKind.description:
A list kind: what every list environment of one name is, how its items
are numbered and which labels are shown beside them.

A list kind states three facts:

- `numbered`: whether its items are numbered. The
  items of a numbered list kind are numbered by the
  `numbering` feature, in a counter
  of the list kind's own (`flm.lists.<kind>`; see
  `CounterDecl`),
  and a reference to one of them shows its number. The items of an
  unnumbered list kind are counted in no counter.
- `labels`: how the label beside an item is written,
  one *label template* per nesting depth. The first template serves a list
  that is inside no list of the same list kind, the second a list nested
  in one such list, and so on; the last template serves every deeper list.
  A label template is written in the language of a counter style's number
  template (`NumberTemplate`):
  every `#{name}` is the item's number in the number format `name`
  (`#{arabic}`, `#{alph}`, `#{roman}`, …), and every other character is
  FLM text written as is, so `(#{roman})` writes `(ii)` for the second
  item. A template that writes no number format, such as `•`, is a *fixed
  label*, shown beside every item.
- `ref_labels`: how a reference to an item writes
  the item's number, one *reference template* per nesting depth, by the
  same rules and in the same language; read for a numbered list kind only.
  The two templates differ where the label carries punctuation that does
  not belong in a sentence: `enumerate` shows `1.` beside its first item,
  and `\ref` to that item shows `Item~1`, because its first label template
  is `#{arabic}.` and its first reference template is `#{arabic}`. The
  constructors `numbered` and
  `unnumbered` give a list kind the same
  templates for both; `ref_labels` sets the
  reference templates separately.

Whether a list kind is numbered is set by `numbered` alone and never
follows from its templates. A numbered list kind may show a fixed label
beside each item; every item still has a number, which a reference to it
or another feature can read. An unnumbered list kind whose label template
writes a number format is refused when the registry is built, since its
items have no number to write. An unnumbered list kind's reference
templates are ignored (neither compiled nor checked), so that switching a
list kind between numbered and unnumbered needs no other change; a
reference to one of its items shows the item's label.

A numbered list kind also has a `nesting` joiner:
what an item of a list nested in another list of the same list kind
writes of the enclosing item's number before its own. By default it
writes nothing, so the second item of a list nested in the second item of
an `enumerate` shows `(ii)`; the template `#{_parent}.` makes it
`2.(ii)`. The enclosing item's number is written through the enclosing
list's reference template, as a reference to that item writes it: `2` for
the shipped `enumerate`, not `2.`. The joiner is data of the numbering
feature, the same `WithinJoinerSpec` that a counter numbered within
another counter declares, and that feature compiles it; see
scoped instances
and the numbering guide.

oneOf.description:
The parent's number, then this joining text, which is FLM: what
`Within::parent` and `Within::joined_by` make. A subsection joined
by `.` is written `1.2`.

The parent is written with its own ancestors before it, each as a part
of its own, so a chain three counters deep is written `1.2.3` with
every counter declaring only its joining text.

A within template, in the language that `Within::template`
describes.

Nothing of the ancestors is written: the counter restarts under its
parent, and its number is shown **bare**, that is, without its
parents' numbers. What `Within::displayed_bare` makes.

The within-joiner registered under this name in
`WITHIN_JOINERS_SLOT`, which writes what its code writes. A name no
feature registers is refused: in a feature's declaration it fails the
registry build, and in a document's numbering options it is the Error
`flm.numbering.unknown-within-joiner`, and the counter keeps the
hierarchy it was declared with.

WithinJoinerSpec.description:
The form of a within-joiner, which writes a counter's ancestors' numbers
before the counter's own number: one of the four forms a `Within` may
carry.

A form is data, not behavior: it can be compared, hashed, and carried in a
document's numbering options. What a form writes is decided when it is
compiled, against the built language and against the within-joiners the
registry holds (`Within::compile`).

xnotes.description: The kinds of xnote (notes set apart from the running text, such as footnotes): for each kind, its commands, the words a reference writes, its label type, whether it is numbered, its number and mark templates, where its notes are shown, how its content is laid out, the title of its list, the text of the link back to the mark and the LaTeX command it is handed to. Fixed when the registry is built: it cannot vary per document or per render.

kinds.description: The xnote kinds, in the order in which their lists are placed.
The xnote kinds, in the order in which their lists are placed.

XnotesConfig.description:
The configuration of the `XnotesFeature`: the xnote
kinds an author writes, in the order in which their lists are placed after
the content.

The default (`XnotesConfig::new`) declares one xnote kind,
`XnoteKind::footnote`: `\footnote{…}`, numbered, listed after the
content under the heading `Footnotes`. A second xnote kind is added by
configuration, with no new syntax:

`XnotesFeature::new` takes this value; the
standard package carries it as
`StdcoreConfig::xnotes`. It is a
feature's configuration: fixed when the registry is built, before any
document is parsed (see settings, options and
configuration),
because the commands are part of the language, whether an xnote is a block
is decided before a document's trees are frozen (no longer changed; see
frozen
trees),
and the counters and
counter styles the feature declares depend on it. The feature therefore
adds `digest_bytes` to the registry digest,
the fingerprint that decides whether a cached result may be reused.

The configuration is checked when the registry is built
(`XnotesConfig::validate`): every xnote kind on its own
(`XnoteKind::validate`), then two kinds of one name, two kinds sharing a
command, and two kinds sharing a label type are refused. A kind with no
command is accepted; no author can write its xnotes. A kind that another
feature contributes (`contribute_kind`) is
checked on its own only: nothing refuses that it shares a label type with
a configured kind.

commands.description:
The commands with which an xnote of the kind is written, without the
backslash; empty for a kind that only another feature creates.

words.description:
The words a reference writes before one number and before several,
with their variants: `Footnote~`, `Footnotes~`.

label_type.description:
The only label type that an xnote of the kind accepts, and the prefix
of its anchors in the output: `fn`. ASCII letters only.

numbered.description: Whether the kind's xnotes are numbered.

number_format.description:
How a reference writes a numbered xnote's number; ignored for an
unnumbered kind. `#{arabic}` by default.

within.description:
The counter within which a numbered kind is numbered, or `None` for
numbering through the whole document; ignored for an unnumbered kind.

mark.description:
The text of the mark, as FLM text: a number template for a numbered
kind (`#{arabic}`), a fixed mark with no number placeholder for an
unnumbered one (empty for no mark).

placement.description: Where the kind's xnotes are shown.

layout.description:
How the content argument is laid out:
`InlineOrBlocks` by default, which makes
a note written on one run inline content and one holding a blank line
or a block paragraphs. `Inline` refuses a blank
line in the note, as every inline argument does.
`Blocks` makes every note paragraphs, even an
empty one: with it, an in-place xnote is always a block of its own,
`\footnote{}` included.

title.description:
The heading placed above the kind's list, as FLM text; `None` for no
heading. The constructors set the plural word, capitalized and without
the non-breaking space (`Footnotes`).

The title is compiled when the registry is built, and a title that is
not valid FLM fails the build. It is read in the language of a counter
style's number template, with no placeholder available: `#` starts a
placeholder there, so a literal `#` is written `\#` or `##`, and a
placeholder such as `#{n}` fails the build.

title_level.description:
The level of the heading above the list, counted from zero like every
heading level; 2 by default.

backlink.description: The text of the link from a listed xnote back to its mark: `↩`.

latex_command.description:
The LaTeX command to which the style file's default definition of
`\flmXN<name>` passes the xnote, without the backslash (`footnote`): a
command of the author's LaTeX, which the author's own preamble may
redefine. ASCII letters only.

XnoteKind.description:
One xnote kind: one way of being an xnote, a piece of text set apart from
the running text (the footnotes written `\footnote{…}`, the side notes a
configuration adds, the notes another feature's elements carry; see the
module documentation of the feature).

An xnote kind states, field by field:

- `name`: what the kind is called, `footnote`. It is
  made of ASCII letters only, because other names are derived from it: the
  counter `flm.xnotes.<name>`, the list element, the LaTeX
  command `\flmXN<name>`.
- `commands`: the commands with which an author
  writes an xnote of the kind, without the backslash: `footnote`. Empty for
  a kind that no author writes, which another feature contributes through
  the service slot of xnote kinds
  (`contribute_kind`).
- `words`: the words a reference writes before an
  xnote's number, `Footnote~` before one number and `Footnotes~` before
  several. `\ref{fn:x}` prints them (`Footnote~1`); the default title of
  the list is made from them; and the accessible name of the link from a
  mark to its xnote begins with them.
- `label_type`: the only label type that an
  xnote of the kind accepts, `fn` in `\label{fn:x}`; also the prefix of
  its anchors in the output (`fn-1`, `fnref--1kzmq`). It is made of ASCII
  letters only, like the name, so that it can be written as the label type
  of a `\label` and begin an anchor.
- `numbered`: whether the kind's xnotes are
  counted, in document order, in a counter of the kind's own. A reference
  to a numbered xnote shows its number; a reference to an unnumbered xnote
  shows its content where that content is inline, and otherwise its label.
- `number_format`: how a reference writes the
  number of a numbered kind's xnote, `#{arabic}`.
- `within`: the counter within which a numbered kind
  is numbered, `None` for numbering through the whole document.
- `mark`: what is shown in the running text where an
  xnote was written. For a numbered kind it is a number template,
  `#{arabic}` by default, and the mark is the xnote's number written
  through it; for an unnumbered kind it is a fixed mark, a template with no
  number placeholder (`*`, `\dag`), or empty for no mark. In both cases
  the template is FLM text, compiled when the registry is built.
- `placement`: listed after the content, or shown
  in place (`XnotePlacement`).
- `layout`: how the content argument is laid out:
  inferred from what the author wrote by default, or fixed.
- `title` and `title_level`:
  the heading placed above the kind's list, and its level.
- `backlink`: the text of the link from the entry
  of a listed xnote back to its mark, `↩`.
- `latex_command`: the LaTeX command to which
  the style file's default definition of `\flmXN<name>` passes the xnote
  (`footnote`), a command of the author's LaTeX that the author's own
  preamble may redefine.

base.description:
The words used when no variant is asked for, and when the variant asked
for is not declared.

PrefixWords.description:
The prefix words of a counter style: the words written before a number by
default, and the named variants that a request may ask for instead.

A variant is a complete pair of words under a name of its own, such as
`capital`, holding `Equation~` and `Equations~` where the default words are
`Eq.~` and `Eqs.~`. A request for a variant the counter style does not
declare (`FormatOptions::variant`) gets the default words; the refs
feature reports such a request at the reference as an Error.

one.description: The word written before a single number.

other.description: The word written before several numbers.

PluralWords.description:
The word written before a number, in two forms: one for a single number
and one for several.

The fields are named after the plural categories `one` and `other` of
natural-language pluralization: `Eq.~` for one equation, `Eqs.~` for
several. Both are FLM, so `~` and a text style mean in them what they mean
in a document.

oneOf.description:
A number template in the template language: every `#{name}` is the
number written in the format `name`, and the rest is written as given:
`#{arabic}.` writes `3.` for the number three, and
`\textbf{#{arabic}}` writes it in bold. A `#{…}` whose name is not a
number format is refused when the counter style is compiled, and so is
a key in brackets, `#[…]{…}`, which only a within template accepts.

A number template in the single-letter language: the first character
among `a`, `A`, `i`, `I` and `1` is the number, written in the format
that character shows by example (letters, capital letters, roman
numerals, capital roman numerals, decimal digits), and the rest is
FLM written as given: `(a)` writes `(c)` for the number three. A text
that holds none of those five characters writes itself for every
number, and the parts of the counters it is numbered within are not
written before it: it is a fixed mark, such as a bullet.

This is the language of an author's own item labels, where the
number's format is shown by an example instead of being named. The
first of the five characters is replaced wherever it is, so `Part a.`
writes `Pcrt a.` for the number three; a text that must hold one of
these characters as a letter of its own is written in the `Formats`
language.

NumberTemplate.description:
A number template: how a counter style writes the number itself, as a text
with a place for the number, written in one of the eight `NumberFormat`s;
a counter style holds one in its field `number_format`.

The text is FLM with a place for the number, in one of two languages, and
it is compiled once, when the counter style is compiled. Around the place
for the number the text is ordinary FLM: `\textbf` and `~` mean in a
number template what they mean in a document.

- `Formats` is written in the template language
  that user definitions use (the template language shared by
  features):
  `#{name}` is the number written in the format `name`. The whole text is
  parsed as one, so markup may surround the number: `\textbf{#{arabic}}`
  writes the number in bold.
- `Initial` is the language of an author's own
  item labels: the first of the characters `a`, `A`, `i`, `I` and `1` is
  the number, written in the format that character shows by example, and
  the rest is FLM: `(a)` writes `(c)` for the number three.

A counter style's number format
(`CounterStyleDecl::number_format`),
each of its sub-levels (`SubLevelDecl`) and a
reference point's own number template
(`NumberSource::number_format`,
always in the `Formats` language) are number templates.

parents.description:
The counter within which this counter is numbered, or the counters any
one of which may be its parent. The parent that applies restarts this
counter: the counter's count is kept separately for each list of
ancestors it is advanced under, each ancestor identified by its name
and its value.

joiner.description:
The within-joiner: how the ancestors' numbers are written before this
counter's own.

no_restart.description:
Whether the parent is left out of what restarts the count. `true`
continues the count across the parent's advances, and the parent's
number is still written before the counter's own (`1.1`, `1.2`,
`2.3`). `false` by default.

Within.description:
The counter within which a counter is numbered, and how that counter's
number is written before the counter's own: the counter's place in the
hierarchy of counters.

A subsection numbered within a section is written `2.3`: the parent is the
counter `flm.headings.section`, and the within-joiner is the joining text
`.`. The two are declared together because the parent decides what
restarts the counter and the within-joiner decides what is shown of the
parent, and neither is of any use without the other. The module
documentation describes the
mechanism.

Three constructors say which counter is the parent:

- `Within::parent`: numbered within that one counter.
- `Within::parents`: numbered within whichever of several counters was
  advanced most recently in document order.
- `Within::parent_set`: the same over the counters of a parent set that
  a feature registered (`ParentSetDecl`).

Each writes the parent's number and a full stop before the counter's own
number, `1.2`. Four builders change what is written:

- `joined_by`: another joining text.
- `template`: a within template, which may write
  markup around an ancestor's number and may refer to more than one
  ancestor.
- `displayed_bare`: nothing of the parent is
  written; the counter restarts under the parent and its number is shown
  bare.
- `joiner_named`: a within-joiner that a feature
  registered by name, which writes what its code writes.

The builder `no_restart` keeps the parent's number
written before the counter's own but stops the parent from restarting the
count: `1.1`, `1.2`, `2.3`.

oneOf.description: Numbered within this one counter.

Numbered within whichever of these counters was advanced most
recently.

Numbered within whichever counter of the parent set of this name was
advanced most recently. A name no feature registers fails the registry
build when a feature declares it, and is the Error
`flm.numbering.unknown-parent-set` when a document's numbering options
give it.

Parents.description:
Which counters a counter may be numbered within: one counter, any counter
of a list, or any counter of a registered parent set.

This is the `parents` field of `Within`, which the constructors
`Within::parent`, `Within::parents` and `Within::parent_set` set.

Where there are several possible parents, the **parent that applies** at a
reference point is the one among them that was advanced most recently in
document order. For example, an equation numbered within any of the
sectioning counters is written `4.1` after a chapter and before the
chapter's first section, and `4.1.2` once a section has begun in that
chapter.

oneOf.description:
The parent's number, then this joining text, which is FLM: what
`Within::parent` and `Within::joined_by` make. A subsection joined
by `.` is written `1.2`.

The parent is written with its own ancestors before it, each as a part
of its own, so a chain three counters deep is written `1.2.3` with
every counter declaring only its joining text.

A within template, in the language that `Within::template`
describes.

Nothing of the ancestors is written: the counter restarts under its
parent, and its number is shown **bare**, that is, without its
parents' numbers. What `Within::displayed_bare` makes.

The within-joiner registered under this name in
`WITHIN_JOINERS_SLOT`, which writes what its code writes. A name no
feature registers is refused: in a feature's declaration it fails the
registry build, and in a document's numbering options it is the Error
`flm.numbering.unknown-within-joiner`, and the counter keeps the
hierarchy it was declared with.

WithinJoinerSpec.description:
The form of a within-joiner, which writes a counter's ancestors' numbers
before the counter's own number: one of the four forms a `Within` may
carry.

A form is data, not behavior: it can be compared, hashed, and carried in a
document's numbering options. What a form writes is decided when it is
compiled, against the built language and against the within-joiners the
registry holds (`Within::compile`).

oneOf.description:
In a list after the document's content: the xnote's mark is placed
where the xnote was written, linked to the xnote's entry in the list.
The default.

Where the xnote is written: one inline span holding the mark and the
content, or, for content holding paragraphs, a block between the two
parts of the paragraph it interrupts.

XnotePlacement.description:
Where the xnotes of an xnote kind are shown: in a list after the
document's content, or where each one is written.

The placement is part of the xnote kind's configuration, fixed when the
registry is built; no render request can change it. The reason is that an
in-place xnote holding paragraphs is a *block* of the document: it
interrupts the paragraph it is written in, as a displayed formula does.
The block-structure pass decides whether
a node is a block before the document's trees are frozen (no longer
changed; see frozen
trees),
from the element value and the node alone, so
the answer is a fact of the document, the same for every output; a listed
xnote is always inline content. A document whose footnotes are listed on
one output and shown in place on another is therefore rendered with two
configurations, that is, with two registries.

oneOf.description:
Inline content: no paragraph is built inside it, and a blank line in it
is an error, reported and read as one space. The default.

A region of blocks: paragraphs are built inside it, exactly as in an
environment body declared `BodyLayout::Blocks`. Content written on
one line becomes one paragraph.

Inferred from the content: a region of blocks when the content holds a
blank line (a paragraph break) or a block-level construct such as a
list, inline content otherwise. This is the rule a fragment laid out
`InlineOrBlocks`
applies to its top level.

ArgLayout.description:
How the block-structure pass lays out an
argument's content: as inline
content, as a region of blocks, or as whichever of the two the content
calls for.

Inline content is running text (words, formulas, commands such as
`\emph{…}`) with no paragraph inside it. A region of blocks holds
paragraphs and block-level constructs such as lists. The layout belongs to
the command's declaration (`ArgDef::layout`); an author cannot choose it
where the command is written.

An argument declared with an opaque wrapper (`ArgDef::opaque_wrapper`)
takes only `Inline`: the block-structure pass carries
its content over as written, so no other layout could take effect. An
argument read in mathematics mode is an opaque
region, which the
block-structure pass carries over untouched, so it may not be declared
`Blocks`. Minting reports a declaration that breaks
either rule
(`MintError::LayoutOnOpaqueWrappedArgument`,
`MintError::BlocksOnMathArgument`).
A layout declared on an argument whose reader yields raw text or places
its content under an opaque wrapper by construction (a verbatim argument, a
characters-only group) is not reported; it has no effect, since the
argument's content is an opaque region.

`arg_layout_of` returns the declared layout of an
argument of a parsed node;
`argument_holds_blocks`
returns whether an argument holds blocks, before and after the
block-structure pass alike.
