defterm.description: The lead-in of a term definition (the `defterm` environment): a template in which `#{term}` is the term being defined, or none for no lead-in. Fixed when the registry is built: it cannot vary per document or per render.

lead_in.description:
The lead-in template, or `None` for no lead-in. `DEFAULT_LEAD_IN`
by default.

The lead-in template, or `None` for no lead-in. `DEFAULT_LEAD_IN`
by default.

DeftermConfig.description:
The configuration of the `Defterm` feature: the
**lead-in**, the text that a term definition (a `defterm` environment)
shows before the words of its first paragraph, usually the term being
defined.

The lead-in is a template in the template
language
(described for authors under the template
language), with one
placeholder: `#{term}` is the term as the term definition writes it,
markup included. The rest of the template is ordinary FLM markup, and
markup may enclose the placeholder. `#{term}: ` is the default, and
`\textbf{Definition} (\emph{#{term}}): ` a richer lead-in. A template
without `#{term}` is allowed: every term definition then opens with the
same words. A template may use `#{term}` once at most, because the term is
shown only once, where the term definition is written.

`None` sets no lead-in: a term definition is then its body alone. A blank
template is not a way to say so: it fails the registry build.

The value is what `Defterm::new` takes, and a host
passes it through
`StdcoreConfig::defterm`. It is
the feature's configuration, fixed when the registry is built (see
settings, options and
configuration):
the template is compiled once then, and a template that does not compile
fails the registry build with a message that quotes it. It enters the
registry digest (`digest_bytes`).

theorems.description: The theorem-like environments: the theorem classes (whether numbered, whether in the shared counter, the heading template, the closing mark, whether a proof's title is read as a back-reference), the theorem kinds (the class, the words, whether a proof is expected), the number format and the label types a numbered kind accepts. Fixed when the registry is built: it cannot vary per document or per render.

kinds.description: The theorem kinds, by environment name.

number_format.description:
The number format every kind's number is written in, a number
template of the numbering feature, `#{arabic}` by default. To write
one kind's number otherwise, a host replaces that kind's counter style
(`flm.theorems.style.<kind>`, see `numbers`) by name
through the numbering feature's configuration.

label_types.description:
The label types that every numbered kind accepts on a `\label` written
on one of its theorems; `DEFAULT_LABEL_TYPES` by default. A theorem
of an unnumbered kind accepts no label.

kinds.description: The theorem kinds, by environment name.

number_format.description:
The number format every kind's number is written in, a number
template of the numbering feature, `#{arabic}` by default. To write
one kind's number otherwise, a host replaces that kind's counter style
(`flm.theorems.style.<kind>`, see `numbers`) by name
through the numbering feature's configuration.

label_types.description:
The label types that every numbered kind accepts on a `\label` written
on one of its theorems; `DEFAULT_LABEL_TYPES` by default. A theorem
of an unnumbered kind accepts no label.

TheoremsConfig.description:
The configuration of the `Theorems` feature: the
theorem classes and the theorem kinds, the number format of every kind,
and the label types every numbered kind accepts.

Every kind is an environment of its own name, `\begin{lemma}…\end{lemma}`,
with no code written for it: a host adds `exercise` by declaring it here.

The default (`TheoremsConfig::new`) declares three classes and eight
kinds:

| class | numbered | counter | closing mark | back-reference | kinds |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `theoremlike` | yes | shared | none | no | `theorem`, `proposition`, `lemma`, `corollary`, `conjecture` |
| `definitionlike` | yes | shared | none | no | `definition`, `remark` |
| `prooflike` | no | — | `□` | yes | `proof` |

with the heading `DEFAULT_HEADING` for every class. `theorem`,
`proposition`, `lemma` and `corollary` expect a proof; the others do not.
`simpleset` and
`richset` are two other complete sets a host
may start from. A host edits any of them through the builders:

The value is what `Theorems::new` takes, and a
host passes it through
`StdcoreConfig::theorems`. It is
the feature's configuration, fixed when the registry is built (see
settings, options and
configuration),
because the environments are part of the language and the counters and
counter styles the feature declares depend on it. For the same reason it
enters the registry digest (`digest_bytes`).

The configuration is checked when the registry is built. The feature's
registration fails, with a message that identifies the class or the kind,
on what `validate` refuses: a kind whose class
the configuration does not declare, a class or kind name that is not a
valid environment name, or a kind that expects a proof but accepts no
label. Once the language is built, the registry build also fails on a
heading template that does not compile, a closing mark that does not
parse and a word that does not parse. A kind whose environment name another
feature already declares is reported as any clash of names in the
registry is.

numbered.description:
Whether the kinds of this class are numbered. A theorem of a numbered
kind is one reference point numbered in the class's counter; a theorem
of an unnumbered kind is a reference point that nothing numbers and that
accepts no label.

shared_counter.description:
For a numbered class, whether its kinds count in the shared counter
`flm.theorems.theorem` (`true`), or each kind in a counter of its own,
`flm.theorems.counter.<kind>` (`false`); see
`numbers`. Unused for an unnumbered class.

heading.description:
The **theorem heading template**: how the heading that opens every
theorem of the class joins the kind's word and number with the
theorem's title. It is written in the template
language
(the language guide describes it for authors under the template
language), with
two placeholders:

- `#{name}` is the kind's word and the theorem's number (`Lemma~4`), or
  the word alone where the theorem has no number;
- `#{title}` is the theorem's title, or, for a class that reads
  back-references, the statement a proof refers to. A theorem with no
  title, or whose back-reference is not shown, binds nothing to
  `#{title}`, so `\IfValueT{#{title}}{…}` tests whether there is one.
  The template may show `#{title}` at most once; an occurrence as the
  test of a conditional (`\IfValueT{#{title}}`) is not counted.

`DEFAULT_HEADING` by default. A template that does not compile fails
the registry build (`heading`). The recomposed LaTeX
does not use the template: LaTeX writes the heading
(`latex`).

closing_mark.description:
The closing mark written at the end of every theorem of the class, as
FLM markup (`□` for the shipped class `prooflike`), or `None` for no
mark. A mark that does not parse fails the registry build.

relation_ref.description:
Whether a title beginning with `*` is read as a back-reference to the
statement the theorem proves: `[*lem:x]` shows the statement's word
and number in the heading, and `[**lem:x]` refers to the same
statement and shows nothing in the heading
(`title_reading`). A class that does not read
back-references takes every title as a title.

TheoremClass.description:
One **theorem class**: what a family of theorem kinds shares. A class
says whether its kinds are numbered and in which counter, how their
heading is written, whether a closing mark ends them, and whether a title
beginning with `*` is read as a back-reference to the statement a theorem
proves.

A class is declared under its name in `TheoremsConfig::classes`, and a
kind refers to it by that name (`TheoremKind::class`). The three shipped
classes are `theoremlike` and `definitionlike`, numbered in the shared
counter, and `prooflike`, unnumbered, closed by the mark `□` and reading a
back-reference from its title (see `TheoremsConfig`). The constructors
`numbered` and
`unnumbered` start a class, and the builders
set its other fields.

class.description:
The name of the kind's theorem class, a key of
`TheoremsConfig::classes`.

words.description:
The kind's words: the word written before the number, singular and
plural, with its named variants.

expects_proof.description:
Whether each statement of this kind should have a proof that refers
back to it, unless the statement carries `\noproofref`. `false` unless
set. The feature's check reports a statement without such a proof
(`check`).

A proof refers back to a statement through one of its labels, so a
kind that expects a proof must accept a label: it must be a kind of a
numbered class, under a configuration declaring at least one of the
`label_types`. A kind of an unnumbered
class accepts no label and could never be proved, so
`TheoremsConfig::validate` refuses such a configuration when the
registry is built.

TheoremKind.description:
One **theorem kind**: one environment an author writes, such as
`theorem`, `lemma`, `proof` or a host's `exercise`. Its key in
`TheoremsConfig::kinds` is the environment's name.

A kind declares its theorem class, its words, and whether each of its
statements expects a proof.

The words are a `PrefixWords` value, the numbering feature's words
written before a number: a base pair (the singular and the plural), which
the heading and a plain `\ref` write, and named variants, each a pair,
which a reference asks for by name (`\ref[abbreviated]{lem:x}`). The base
pair of every shipped kind is the capitalized form (`Lemma`, `Lemmas`),
and every shipped kind declares the variants `LOWERCASE_VARIANT`,
`CAPITAL_VARIANT` and `ABBREVIATED_VARIANT`. The words are FLM markup
and hold no space before the number: the kind's counter style writes a
non-breaking space after each (`numbers`). The base
singular word is also the word a heading shows alone where the theorem
has no number, and the display name the recomposed LaTeX gives the
environment in its declaration (`Lemma` in `\newtheorem{lemma}{Lemma}`).

base.description:
The words used when no variant is asked for, and when the variant asked
for is not declared.

PrefixWords.description:
The prefix words of a counter style: the words written before a number by
default, and the named variants that a request may ask for instead.

A variant is a complete pair of words under a name of its own, such as
`capital`, holding `Equation~` and `Equations~` where the default words are
`Eq.~` and `Eqs.~`. A request for a variant the counter style does not
declare (`FormatOptions::variant`) gets the default words; the refs
feature reports such a request at the reference as an Error.

one.description: The word written before a single number.

other.description: The word written before several numbers.

PluralWords.description:
The word written before a number, in two forms: one for a single number
and one for several.

The fields are named after the plural categories `one` and `other` of
natural-language pluralization: `Eq.~` for one equation, `Eqs.~` for
several. Both are FLM, so `~` and a text style mean in them what they mean
in a document.

oneOf.description:
A number template in the template language: every `#{name}` is the
number written in the format `name`, and the rest is written as given:
`#{arabic}.` writes `3.` for the number three, and
`\textbf{#{arabic}}` writes it in bold. A `#{…}` whose name is not a
number format is refused when the counter style is compiled, and so is
a key in brackets, `#[…]{…}`, which only a within template accepts.

A number template in the single-letter language: the first character
among `a`, `A`, `i`, `I` and `1` is the number, written in the format
that character shows by example (letters, capital letters, roman
numerals, capital roman numerals, decimal digits), and the rest is
FLM written as given: `(a)` writes `(c)` for the number three. A text
that holds none of those five characters writes itself for every
number, and the parts of the counters it is numbered within are not
written before it: it is a fixed mark, such as a bullet.

This is the language of an author's own item labels, where the
number's format is shown by an example instead of being named. The
first of the five characters is replaced wherever it is, so `Part a.`
writes `Pcrt a.` for the number three; a text that must hold one of
these characters as a letter of its own is written in the `Formats`
language.

NumberTemplate.description:
A number template: how a counter style writes the number itself, as a text
with a place for the number, written in one of the eight `NumberFormat`s;
a counter style holds one in its field `number_format`.

The text is FLM with a place for the number, in one of two languages, and
it is compiled once, when the counter style is compiled. Around the place
for the number the text is ordinary FLM: `\textbf` and `~` mean in a
number template what they mean in a document.

- `Formats` is written in the template language
  that user definitions use (the template language shared by
  features):
  `#{name}` is the number written in the format `name`. The whole text is
  parsed as one, so markup may surround the number: `\textbf{#{arabic}}`
  writes the number in bold.
- `Initial` is the language of an author's own
  item labels: the first of the characters `a`, `A`, `i`, `I` and `1` is
  the number, written in the format that character shows by example, and
  the rest is FLM: `(a)` writes `(c)` for the number three.

A counter style's number format
(`CounterStyleDecl::number_format`),
each of its sub-levels (`SubLevelDecl`) and a
reference point's own number template
(`NumberSource::number_format`,
always in the `Formats` language) are number templates.

quote.description: The quote environments, by name: for each, the quotation-section commands its body accepts (`text`, `lines`, `attributed`, `block`) and the kind of quotation section that content written outside those commands is read as (the key `bare`; when it is absent, such content is an error). Fixed when the registry is built: it cannot vary per document or per render.

QuoteConfig.description:
The configuration of the `Quote` feature: the quote
environments, each environment's name mapped to its `QuoteEnvironment`.

The default (`QuoteConfig::new`) declares three environments:

| environment | quotation-section commands | bare content read as |
|---|---|---|
| `quote` | `\text`, `\lines`, `\attributed`, `\block` | an error |
| `blockquote` | none | one block section |
| `address` | none | one lines section |

A host declares others, or changes these, through the same type:

The value is what `Quote::new` takes; a host using
the standard package passes it with
`StdcoreConfig::quote`. The
configuration is fixed when the registry is built, before any document is
parsed
(configuration),
because the environments and their quotation-section commands are part of
the language. The feature therefore feeds
`digest_bytes` into the registry
digest, the number that changes whenever something
about the registry that can change what processing produces changes
(`FeatureBuilder::digest_input`).

The feature checks the configuration when the registry is built
(`validate`), and the registry build fails, with
a message that identifies the environment, on any of these: a name that
is empty or holds whitespace, a brace, a backslash or `%`; a name equal to
one of the kind tokens a presentation list reserves (`LIST_RESERVED_KINDS`), since an
environment's name becomes the kind token of the block it is staged as;
and an environment that accepts no quotation-section command and reads no
bare content. A name that another feature also declares, such as `itemize`
or `theorem`, makes the registry build fail as any two declarations of one
name do.

The configuration refers to no backend, HTML tag or stylesheet: the
lowering rules and stylesheets of each backend decide how a quotation is
presented.

sections.description: The quotation-section commands the body accepts.

bare.description:
The kind of quotation section bare content is read as; `None` makes
bare content an error.

QuoteEnvironment.description:
One quote environment: the quotation-section commands its body accepts,
and the kind of quotation section its **bare content** (content written in
the body outside any quotation-section command) is read as.

An environment accepts exactly the quotation-section commands of
`sections`, a set: the other commands are
not declared in its body, and the order of the set has no meaning (an
author writes the quotation sections in any order). Where
`bare` holds a kind, each run of bare content is
read as one quotation section of that kind; where it holds none, bare
content is an error (the condition
`BareContent`). An environment must accept a
quotation-section command or read bare content, or
`QuoteConfig::validate` refuses the configuration when the registry is
built.

The bare-content kind also decides how the body is laid out
(`holds_blocks`): as paragraphs and
blocks when it is `Block` or when there is none, so
that each quotation-section command is a block of its own; as inline
content when it is `Text`,
`Lines` or `Attributed`,
so that the quotation sections and the bare content form one run.

oneOf.description: A quoted passage, one paragraph, written `\text{…}`.
Lines set as written, written `\lines{…}`.
The attribution, written `\attributed{…}`.
Paragraphs and blocks, written `\block{…}`.

QuoteSection.description:
The kind of one quotation section of a quote environment, and the
quotation-section command that writes it.

- `Text` — a quoted passage, one paragraph:
  `\text{…}`.
- `Lines` — content set line by line, each `\\`
  ending a line and each `\indent` at the start of a line indenting it by
  one tab: `\lines{…}`.
- `Attributed` — the attribution, an author or
  a source: `\attributed{…}`.
- `Block` — ordinary paragraphs and blocks set as a
  quotation: `\block{…}`.

annotations.description:
The annotators, in order, the first numbered 0: for each, the name of its command (without the backslash) and the initials shown at the start of its annotations. Fixed when the registry is built: it cannot vary per document or per render.

Whether every annotation is left out of the output, each highlight shown as its passage alone and each comment not at all (`hidden`, false by default). Set per render request.

annotators.description:
The annotators, in order: the first is annotator 0. In settings, a map
from each annotator's command name to its other fields.

hidden.description:
Whether every annotation is left out of the output, each highlight
shown as its passage alone and each comment not at all. `false` by
default.

annotators.description:
The annotators, in order: the first is annotator 0. In settings, a map
from each annotator's command name to its other fields.

AnnotationsConfig.description:
The configuration of the `annotations` feature: the annotators, in order.

Each annotator declares one command, written in three forms: `\phf{…}`
and `\phf … \endphf` mark a passage (a **highlight**), and `\phf[…]`
writes a remark (a **comment**). The order numbers the annotators from
zero; an output that shows colors chooses one per number. The default
configuration declares **no annotator**, and the feature then declares no
command at all: `\phf` is an unknown command until a host configures it.

initials.description:
The initials shown at the start of the annotator's annotations, such as
`PhF`; `None` for none.

Annotator.description:
One annotator: a reviewer who highlights passages and writes remarks in a
document, with the command they write and the initials shown at the start
of each of their annotations.

- `command` — the name of the annotator's command,
  without the backslash: `phf` makes `\phf{…}` (a highlight), `\phf[…]` (a
  comment) and `\phf … \endphf` (a highlight). It must be made of ASCII
  letters only, like every command name of the language written with
  letters, and must be neither `begin` nor `end`, which open and close
  environments (`Annotator::validate`).
- `initials` — the short text shown where each of
  the annotator's highlights and comments starts (in the margin, on an
  output that has one), such as `PhF`; `None` for an annotator whose
  annotations show no initials. The text is shown as written, never read
  as markup.

An annotator's **number** is its position in
`AnnotationsConfig::annotators`, counting from zero. The configuration
specifies no color: an output that shows colors chooses one per number
(the HTML stylesheet `flm.annotations.style` and the `phfcc` LaTeX package
give the first eight numbers their own colors).

hidden.description:
Whether every annotation is left out of the output, each highlight
shown as its passage alone and each comment not at all. `false` by
default.

AnnotationsRenderOptions.description:
The render options of the `annotations` feature: an option type whose
values are set on a render request (`crate::model::options`), in the
plan request's overrides (`Overrides`), as
the example shows.

When `hidden` is true, every annotation is
left out of the output on every backend: a highlight is shown as its
passage alone and a comment as nothing. This gives a clean copy of an
annotated document without any change to its source.

graphics.description:
Whether `\includegraphics` is also an ordinary command of the document (`global`, false by default), besides a command of the scoped package `flm.graphics.includegraphics`, which a float type can make available in its body (the `figure` and `table` types do). Fixed when the registry is built: it cannot vary per document or per render.

How each output publishes its images (`strategy`: `reference`, `copy` or `data-uri`), the conversion rules it applies (`convert`), and the factors by which it multiplies the size of raster and of vector images (`magnification`: `raster` and `vector`, 1 by default), each a map from an output's name to its value. Set per render request.

global.description:
Whether `\includegraphics` is also an ordinary command of the
document, which can be written wherever text can, besides a command of
its scoped package. `false` by default.

strategy.description:
How each output publishes its images, by the output's name:
`reference` (the address of the file where it is, the default), `copy`
(a copy of the file beside the output) or `data-uri` (the file's
content written into the address). `copy` and `data-uri` need a way to
read image files, which the program must supply.

convert.description:
The conversion rules of each output, by the output's name, applied
under `copy` and `data-uri` and never under `reference`. Each rule has
`from` (a format or a list of formats among `png`, `jpeg`, `gif`,
`webp`, `svg`, `pdf`), `to` (one format), `via` (the names of the
converters allowed; any converter where empty) and `options` (`dpi`,
`transparent_bg`). For each image, the first rule whose `from` lists
the image's format applies. No rule by default.

magnification.description:
The magnification of each output, by the output's name: `raster` and
`vector`, each a number greater than zero (1 where not given), by
which every dimension of a raster or a vector image shown on that
output is multiplied, including the `width` and `height` the author
gave. An image whose type is not known uses `vector`. No
magnification by default.

global.description:
Whether `\includegraphics` is also an ordinary command of the
document, which can be written wherever text can, besides a command of
its scoped package. `false` by default.

GraphicsConfig.description:
The configuration of the `graphics` feature: whether `\includegraphics`
is also an ordinary command of the document.

Under the default, `global: false`, the command can be written only inside
the bodies whose declarations refer to the scoped package
`INCLUDEGRAPHICS_PACKAGE`, such as a `figure`'s body when the `floats`
feature is registered. Under `global: true`, it is also an ordinary
command, which can be written wherever text can. In both cases an image is
inline content, except as a direct child of a float's body, where it is a
block.

A feature's configuration is the plain Rust value the feature is
constructed from; it is fixed when the registry is built and cannot vary
per document or per render (settings, options and
configuration).
This one decides which commands the language has, so the feature adds
`digest_bytes` to the registry digest. The
standard package takes it through
`StdcoreConfig::graphics`.

strategy.description:
How each output publishes its images, by the output's name:
`reference` (the address of the file where it is, the default), `copy`
(a copy of the file beside the output) or `data-uri` (the file's
content written into the address). `copy` and `data-uri` need a way to
read image files, which the program must supply.

convert.description:
The conversion rules of each output, by the output's name, applied
under `copy` and `data-uri` and never under `reference`. Each rule has
`from` (a format or a list of formats among `png`, `jpeg`, `gif`,
`webp`, `svg`, `pdf`), `to` (one format), `via` (the names of the
converters allowed; any converter where empty) and `options` (`dpi`,
`transparent_bg`). For each image, the first rule whose `from` lists
the image's format applies. No rule by default.

magnification.description:
The magnification of each output, by the output's name: `raster` and
`vector`, each a number greater than zero (1 where not given), by
which every dimension of a raster or a vector image shown on that
output is multiplied, including the `width` and `height` the author
gave. An image whose type is not known uses `vector`. No
magnification by default.

GraphicsRenderOptions.description:
The render options of the `graphics` feature: for each output, how its
images are published, which conversion rules apply, and by how much its
images are magnified.

An option type is a plain Rust struct a feature declares once; its values
are set on a document or on a render request
(`crate::model::options`). This one is set on the render request. Each
field is a map from an output's name (`html`, `latex-recomposed`, `text`)
to that output's value; an output that a map does not list takes the
default. When a host combines several sources of settings, a source that
writes one output's entry leaves the other outputs' entries as the
lower-ranked sources wrote them. The publish stage of a backend reads the
entries of the output of the backend's name: each standard backend makes
one output, named after the backend.

oneOf.description:
The address of the file where it is: the graphics resolver's address
where a resolver found the file, else the path as written. Nothing is
read, copied or converted. The default.

A copy of the file, converted where a conversion rule says so, is made
part of the output, and the address is the copy's, as the host's
artifact namer gives it. Needs a graphics resolver to read the file, an
artifact namer, and an output that can hold several files (not the
plain-text output).

The file's content, converted where a conversion rule says so, is
written into the address itself, `data:<media type>;base64,<content>`,
so that the output needs no other file. Needs a graphics resolver to
read the file, and an output that can show such an address (the HTML
page only).

Strategy.description:
How an output publishes its images: one of the three strategies. In
settings, written `reference`, `copy` or `data-uri`. See the module
documentation.

from.description:
The formats the rule turns into `to`: one format (`pdf`) or a list
(`[svg, pdf]`), each one of `png`, `jpeg`, `gif`, `webp`, `svg` and
`pdf`.

to.description: The format the rule turns them into.

via.description:
The names of the converters allowed to perform the rule, in no
particular order; where the list is empty (the default), every
converter is allowed.

options.description:
The options the converter reads, such as the resolution at which a
drawing is turned into pixels.

ConversionRule.description:
A conversion rule: which formats are turned into which, by which
converters, with which options. See the module
documentation.

In settings, a rule is written as a map with the keys `from`, `to`, `via`
and `options`; `from` and `to` are required.

anyOf.description: One format.
A list of formats.

Formats.description:
One format or a list of formats, as a rule's `from` is written in
settings.

oneOf.description: A PNG image, `image/png`: a grid of pixels.
A JPEG image, `image/jpeg`: a grid of pixels.
A GIF image, `image/gif`: a grid of pixels, possibly animated.
A WebP image, `image/webp`: a grid of pixels.
An SVG drawing, `image/svg+xml`.
A PDF document, `application/pdf`, whose first page is the drawing.

ImageFormat.description:
The format of an image file that a conversion rule can list: one of the
six kinds of image the library knows by name.

A file of another kind is still published, under its own media type, but
no conversion rule can list it and no converter is asked about it. In
settings, a format is written by its short name
(`name`): `png`, `jpeg`, `gif`, `webp`, `svg`,
`pdf`.

dpi.description:
The resolution, in dots per inch, at which a drawing (an SVG or a PDF
image) is turned into pixels. Where it is not given, the converter
chooses.

transparent_bg.description:
Whether a drawing turned into pixels keeps a transparent background,
where the converter can do so. Where it is not given, the converter
chooses.

ConversionOptions.description:
The options of a conversion rule, which the converter that performs the
rule reads. In settings, the rule's `options`, with the keys `dpi` and
`transparent_bg`.

raster.description: The factor of a raster image.

vector.description: The factor of a vector image, and of an image whose type is not known.

Magnification.description:
The magnification of one output: the factor by which the size of each
image shown on it is multiplied, one for raster images (a grid of pixels,
such as a PNG or JPEG file) and one for vector images (a drawing, such as
an SVG or PDF file). In settings, `{raster: 1.5, vector: 1.25}`; a factor
not given is 1.

The two factors let an output show images at another size relative to its
text than the other outputs do, such as larger on a web page than in a
printed document. See `GraphicsRenderOptions::magnification`.

floats.description: The float types, each an environment of the type's name: its caption name, its numbering policy, its number format, the words a reference writes before its number, the content handlers it accepts, the scoped packages available in its body and the label types it accepts. Fixed when the registry is built: it cannot vary per document or per render.

types.description:
The float types, in order; no two have the same name. In settings, a
map from each type's name to its fields.

The float types, in order; no two have the same name. In settings, a
map from each type's name to its fields.

FloatsConfig.description:
The configuration of the `Floats` feature: the float
types it declares, in order.

The default (`FloatsConfig::new`) declares the two shipped types,
`figure` and `table`, both
numbered. A caller replaces a type by declaring one of the same name
(`float_type`), removes one
(`without_type`), adds its own, or starts
from `FloatsConfig::empty`:

A float type is document structure (a numbered series and the word under
its content), not a property of the content that fills it. The two shipped
types are therefore declared here, and they refer to the content handlers
they accept by name. A feature that brings a float type together with its
own content declares the type through
`contribute_type` instead.

The value is what `Floats::new` takes; the standard
package takes it through
`StdcoreConfig::floats`. It is a
configuration, fixed when the registry is built: the environments are part
of the language, and the counters and counter styles are built from it. The
feature therefore adds `digest_bytes` to the
registry digest. The feature checks it when it registers
(`validate`).

caption_name.description:
The word written before the number in the line under a numbered
float's content: `Figure` in `Figure 1: A photo`. Plain text, shown as
written.

numbering.description:
When a float of the type is numbered: `numbered`, `unnumbered` or
`auto-numbered` (numbered when it carries a `\label`; the default).

words.description:
The words a reference writes before the number (`Fig.~` in `Fig.~1`),
singular and plural, with their variants (`Figure~` in `Figure~1`,
written by `\ref[S]{…}`). FLM markup.

handlers.description:
The names of the content handlers the type accepts, tried in this
order: the first that accepts a float's content decides. A handler that
no registered feature contributes accepts nothing. At least one name;
`any` accepts any content.

scoped_packages.description:
The names of the scoped packages available in the body of a float of
the type, besides the package of `\caption`, `\label` and
`\nonumber`: they make the commands of the type's content available
there (`\includegraphics` in a `figure`). A package that no registered
feature declares makes nothing available.

label_types.description:
The label types a `\label` in a float of the type may have (the part
before the colon); by default the type's own name.

FloatType.description:
One **float type**: one environment an author writes, such as `figure`,
`table`, or a `diagram` that a host configures. A float type has a
numbering policy, a caption name (written before its number in the line
under its content), a number format, the words a reference writes before
its number, the content handlers it accepts, the scoped packages available
in its body and the label types it accepts.

`FloatType::new` gives a type the defaults its name implies: numbered
when it carries a `\label` (`FloatNumbering::AutoNumbered`), the number
written in arabic digits, the caption name and the words derived from the
capitalized name (`diagram` gives the caption name `Diagram` and the
words `Diagram~`, `Diagrams~`, with the same pair as the variant
`capital`), no scoped package, and one accepted label type, the type's own
name (`\label{diagram:x}`). The
builder methods change each field. `FloatType::figure` and
`FloatType::table` are the two shipped types.

A float type is declared through the configuration (`FloatsConfig`) or by
another feature through `contribute_type`. Its
name must consist of ASCII letters and must not be one of the reserved kind
tokens (`validate`).

In settings, a float type is one entry of the map `types`, under its name;
`handlers` must be written, and every other field takes the default that
`FloatType::new` gives for that name and those handlers.

oneOf.description:
Every float of the type is numbered, unless it carries `\nonumber`, as
a displayed equation is.

No float of the type is numbered, regardless of its `\label` and
`\nonumber`; a `\nonumber` in one changes nothing and is reported
with a Note.

A float of the type is numbered when it carries a `\label` and no
`\nonumber`; a `\nonumber` in a float with no `\label` changes nothing
and is reported with a Note. The default.

FloatNumbering.description:
The **numbering policy** of a float type: when the floats of the type are
numbered.

A float is numbered in its type's counter or not at all. The policy and the
float's own `\label` and `\nonumber` decide which
(`numbers`); where the numbering feature is not
registered, a float that the policy numbers is reported
(`NoNumbering`) and shown without a number, except on
the recomposed LaTeX, where LaTeX numbers it. In settings, the policy is written
`numbered`, `unnumbered` or `auto-numbered`.

oneOf.description:
A number template in the template language: every `#{name}` is the
number written in the format `name`, and the rest is written as given:
`#{arabic}.` writes `3.` for the number three, and
`\textbf{#{arabic}}` writes it in bold. A `#{…}` whose name is not a
number format is refused when the counter style is compiled, and so is
a key in brackets, `#[…]{…}`, which only a within template accepts.

A number template in the single-letter language: the first character
among `a`, `A`, `i`, `I` and `1` is the number, written in the format
that character shows by example (letters, capital letters, roman
numerals, capital roman numerals, decimal digits), and the rest is
FLM written as given: `(a)` writes `(c)` for the number three. A text
that holds none of those five characters writes itself for every
number, and the parts of the counters it is numbered within are not
written before it: it is a fixed mark, such as a bullet.

This is the language of an author's own item labels, where the
number's format is shown by an example instead of being named. The
first of the five characters is replaced wherever it is, so `Part a.`
writes `Pcrt a.` for the number three; a text that must hold one of
these characters as a letter of its own is written in the `Formats`
language.

NumberTemplate.description:
A number template: how a counter style writes the number itself, as a text
with a place for the number, written in one of the eight `NumberFormat`s;
a counter style holds one in its field `number_format`.

for the number the text is ordinary FLM: `\textbf` and `~` mean in a
number template what they mean in a document.

  that user definitions use (the template language shared by
  features):

base.description:
The words used when no variant is asked for, and when the variant asked
for is not declared.

PrefixWords.description:
The prefix words of a counter style: the words written before a number by
default, and the named variants that a request may ask for instead.

A variant is a complete pair of words under a name of its own, such as
`capital`, holding `Equation~` and `Equations~` where the default words are
`Eq.~` and `Eqs.~`. A request for a variant the counter style does not
declare (`FormatOptions::variant`) gets the default words; the refs
feature reports such a request at the reference as an Error.

one.description: The word written before a single number.

other.description: The word written before several numbers.

PluralWords.description:
The word written before a number, in two forms: one for a single number
and one for several.

The fields are named after the plural categories `one` and `other` of
natural-language pluralization: `Eq.~` for one equation, `Eqs.~` for
several. Both are FLM, so `~` and a text style mean in them what they mean
in a document.

cells.description: Whether the `cells` environment can be written wherever blocks can (`global`, false by default), in addition to the bodies that refer to the scoped package `flm.cells.environment`, such as a `table` float's. Fixed when the registry is built: it cannot vary per document or per render.

global.description:
Whether the `cells` environment is an ordinary environment of the
document, in addition to its declaration in the scoped package
`ENVIRONMENT_PACKAGE`. `false` by default.

Whether the `cells` environment is an ordinary environment of the
document, in addition to its declaration in the scoped package
`ENVIRONMENT_PACKAGE`. `false` by default.

CellsConfig.description:
The configuration of the `cells` feature: whether the `cells` environment
is also an ordinary environment of the document.

Under the default, `global: false`, the environment can be written only
inside the bodies whose declarations refer to the scoped package
`ENVIRONMENT_PACKAGE`: a `table` float's, where the `floats` feature is
registered. Under `global: true` it is also an ordinary environment,
written wherever blocks can be: between paragraphs, in a list item, in a
footnote.

The value is the feature's configuration (see
configuration):
fixed when the registry is built, since it decides which environments the
registry's parsing language (`BuiltLang`)
holds, and fed into the registry digest
(`digest_bytes`). The standard package
carries it as `StdcoreConfig::cells`.

citations.description: Where the citation entries are shown (`placement`: `listed` after the content, or `in-place` in the citation marks), how a citation mark shows its numbers (`mark`: `bracketed` or `superscript`), the citation counter style (`style`: the number format, the delimiters, the texts joining several numbers, whether consecutive numbers make a range, and the words `\R` writes), the heading above the list of cited works (`heading_title`, or null for no heading, and `heading_level`), and the text written between the numbers and a note (`note_separator`). Fixed when the registry is built: it cannot vary per document or per render.

placement.description:
Where the citation entries are shown: listed after the content, the
default, or in the citation marks in place of the numbers
(`CitationPlacement`).

mark.description:
How a citation mark shows its numbers under the listed placement, and
how the list of cited works labels its entries: `MarkForm::Bracketed`
by default. It has no effect under `CitationPlacement::InPlace`.

style.description:
The citation counter style, a counter style
(`CounterStyleDecl`): how a number is written, the delimiters, the
texts joining several numbers, whether consecutive numbers make a
range, and the words `\R` writes before a citation mark. By default
(`default_style`): arabic numbers, `[` and `]`, the compact join,
ranges on, the words `ref.~` and `refs.~`, and the variant `capital`
with the words `Ref.~` and `Refs.~`.

In settings data, the fields written replace those of the default
citation counter style, and the name is not written: it is always
`STYLE_NAME`.

heading_title.description:
The title of the heading above the list of cited works, as FLM text:
`References` by default; `None` for a list with no heading above it
(`without_heading`).

heading_level.description:
The level of the heading above the list of cited works, counted from
zero like every heading level; 2 by default, the level of the heading
above a list of footnotes. The feature passes it to the heading
unchanged, and accepts every value. It has no effect on a list with no
heading.

note_separator.description:
The text written between a group's numbers and its note, as FLM text:
`; ` by default, as in `[1; Thm 4]`.

Where the citation entries are shown: listed after the content, the
default, or in the citation marks in place of the numbers
(`CitationPlacement`).

mark.description:
How a citation mark shows its numbers under the listed placement, and
how the list of cited works labels its entries: `MarkForm::Bracketed`
by default. It has no effect under `CitationPlacement::InPlace`.

style.description:
The citation counter style, a counter style
(`CounterStyleDecl`): how a number is written, the delimiters, the
texts joining several numbers, whether consecutive numbers make a
range, and the words `\R` writes before a citation mark. By default

with the words `Ref.~` and `Refs.~`.

In settings data, the fields written replace those of the default
citation counter style, and the name is not written: it is always
`STYLE_NAME`.

The title of the heading above the list of cited works, as FLM text:
`References` by default; `None` for a list with no heading above it
(`without_heading`).

The level of the heading above the list of cited works, counted from
zero like every heading level; 2 by default, the level of the heading
above a list of footnotes. The feature passes it to the heading
unchanged, and accepts every value. It has no effect on a list with no

The text written between a group's numbers and its note, as FLM text:
`; ` by default, as in `[1; Thm 4]`.

CitationsConfig.description:
The configuration of the `citations` feature: where the citation entries are
shown, the form of a citation mark, the citation counter style, the heading
of the list of cited works, and the text between the numbers and a note.

It is the plain Rust value the feature is constructed from
(`Citations::new`), fixed when the registry is
built (configuration).
It enters the registry digest
(`digest_bytes`), and its texts are
compiled when the registry is built: a text that is not valid FLM fails
the build with a message that identifies the text. The standard package
takes it as
`StdcoreConfig::citations`.

The citation counter style is the feature's own: the counter styles a host
sets in the numbering feature's configuration
(`NumberingConfig::styles`)
do not replace it, and a host changes it here.

oneOf.description:
Listed after the content, under a heading, one citation entry per cited
work in the order of the numbers; a citation mark shows the numbers of
its works, as its form (`MarkForm`) says. The default.

In place: a citation mark shows the citation entries themselves, one
group per item between the citation counter style's delimiters (`[Knuth,
1984][Lamport, 1994; Thm 4]`), and no list is placed. The form of a
citation mark has no effect.

CitationPlacement.description:
Where the citation entries of the cited works are shown. In settings data,
`listed` or `in-place`.

oneOf.description:
The numbers inline, between the citation counter style's delimiters:
`text [1,3–5]`, with a no-break space written before the citation mark
of a `\cite`. The default.

The numbers raised, with no delimiters: `text¹˒³⁻⁵`, with nothing
written before the citation mark of a `\cite`. A citation written with
`\R` is never raised: its numbers are shown inline, with no delimiters
(`refs.~1,2`).

MarkForm.description:
How a citation mark shows the numbers of the works its citation chunk
cites, where the citation entries are listed after the content
(`CitationPlacement::Listed`); it has no effect under the in-place
placement. In settings data, `bracketed` or `superscript`.

The form decides the delimiters wherever numbers are shown. Under the
bracketed form, a citation mark and an entry's label in the list of cited
works carry the citation counter style's delimiters; under the superscript
form they carry none.

number_format.description: The number template: how the number itself is written.

sub_levels.description:
The sub-levels, outermost first. A value cannot be written with a
sub-number at a level the counter style does not declare.

prefix_words.description: The prefix words: the word written before the number.

delimiters.description: The delimiters: the texts around the number.

join.description: The join texts: the texts that join several numbers.

name_in_link.description:
Whether the word before the numbers is part of the link to the first
number written. With one number written by `format()`, the whole
text is one link regardless of this setting. On by default.

repeat_parents_in_range.description:
Whether the end of a range repeats the part of the number that comes
from the counters it is numbered within: `A.I–A.III` instead of
`A.I–III`. Off by default.

ranges.description:
Whether consecutive numbers collapse into a range: `1–3` when on,
`1,2,3` when off. Several numbers are sorted in both cases, and when
off every number is written separately, each with a link of its own.
On by default.

number_writer.description:
The name of the number writer that writes this
counter style's numbers, registered under that name in
`NUMBER_WRITERS_SLOT`, or `None` for the
default writer. A name no feature registers fails the registry build.

CounterStyleDecl.description:
A counter style, as a feature declares it.

A counter style says how a counter value is shown: the number template, the
sub-levels, the prefix words with their variants, the delimiters and the
join texts, each text written in FLM and parsed once, when the counter
style is compiled against the built language
(`compile`) into a `CounterStyle`. It also
holds three choices about links and ranges, and may ask for a number writer
other than the default one. The concepts overview presents counters and
counter styles together (counters and counter
styles).

A feature contributes the declaration to the service slot
`STYLES_SLOT`; a counter refers to its default counter
style by name (`CounterDecl::default_style`),
and a reference point gives the counter style of its number in its number
source. A host replaces a declared counter style by name through
`NumberingConfig`.

A counter style's name is a dotted name owned by the feature that declares
it, such as `flm.math.style.equation`, so that two features may each
declare a counter style for the same counter without a clash.

oneOf.description:
A number template in the template language: every `#{name}` is the
number written in the format `name`, and the rest is written as given:
`#{arabic}.` writes `3.` for the number three, and
`\textbf{#{arabic}}` writes it in bold. A `#{…}` whose name is not a
number format is refused when the counter style is compiled, and so is
a key in brackets, `#[…]{…}`, which only a within template accepts.

A number template in the single-letter language: the first character
among `a`, `A`, `i`, `I` and `1` is the number, written in the format
that character shows by example (letters, capital letters, roman
numerals, capital roman numerals, decimal digits), and the rest is
FLM written as given: `(a)` writes `(c)` for the number three. A text
that holds none of those five characters writes itself for every
number, and the parts of the counters it is numbered within are not
written before it: it is a fixed mark, such as a bullet.

This is the language of an author's own item labels, where the
number's format is shown by an example instead of being named. The
first of the five characters is replaced wherever it is, so `Part a.`
writes `Pcrt a.` for the number three; a text that must hold one of
these characters as a letter of its own is written in the `Formats`
language.

NumberTemplate.description:
A number template: how a counter style writes the number itself, as a text
with a place for the number, written in one of the eight `NumberFormat`s;
a counter style holds one in its field `number_format`.

The text is FLM with a place for the number, in one of two languages, and
it is compiled once, when the counter style is compiled. Around the place
for the number the text is ordinary FLM: `\textbf` and `~` mean in a
number template what they mean in a document.

- `Formats` is written in the template language
  that user definitions use (the template language shared by
  features):
  `#{name}` is the number written in the format `name`. The whole text is
  parsed as one, so markup may surround the number: `\textbf{#{arabic}}`
  writes the number in bold.
- `Initial` is the language of an author's own
  item labels: the first of the characters `a`, `A`, `i`, `I` and `1` is
  the number, written in the format that character shows by example, and
  the rest is FLM: `(a)` writes `(c)` for the number three.

A counter style's number format
(`CounterStyleDecl::number_format`),
each of its sub-levels (`SubLevelDecl`) and a
reference point's own number template
(`NumberSource::number_format`,
always in the `Formats` language) are number templates.

separator.description:
The text written before this level's number, when something is
written before it.

number_format.description: How this level's number is written.

SubLevelDecl.description:
A sub-level of a counter style: how the sub-numbers at one level are
written, and the separator written before each.

A counter style with one sub-level, declared as letters after a full stop,
writes the value `(3, 2)` as `3.b`. The separator is FLM; it is left out
when nothing has been written before the sub-number, so that the end of a
range is written `b` and not `.b`.

base.description:
The words used when no variant is asked for, and when the variant asked
for is not declared.

PrefixWords.description:
The prefix words of a counter style: the words written before a number by
default, and the named variants that a request may ask for instead.

A variant is a complete pair of words under a name of its own, such as
`capital`, holding `Equation~` and `Equations~` where the default words are
`Eq.~` and `Eqs.~`. A request for a variant the counter style does not
declare (`FormatOptions::variant`) gets the default words; the refs
feature reports such a request at the reference as an Error.

one.description: The word written before a single number.

other.description: The word written before several numbers.

PluralWords.description:
The word written before a number, in two forms: one for a single number
and one for several.

The fields are named after the plural categories `one` and `other` of
natural-language pluralization: `Eq.~` for one equation, `Eqs.~` for
several. Both are FLM, so `~` and a text style mean in them what they mean
in a document.

open.description: The text written before the number.

close.description: The text written after the number.

Delimiters.description:
The delimiters of a counter style: the text before and the text after a
number, such as `(` and `)` for an equation number shown as `(3)`.

Both are FLM, and both are left out when a number is asked for without
delimiters (`FormatOptions::without_delimiters`).

one_pre.description: Before a single run. Default: empty.

one_post.description: After a single run. Default: empty.

range_pre.description: Before a run of several numbers. Default: empty.

range_mid.description: Between the ends of a run of three or more. Default: `${endash}`.

range_pairmid.description:
Between the ends of a run of exactly two. Default: `${sep}`; compact:
`,`.

range_post.description: After a run of several numbers. Default: empty.

list_pre.description: Before three runs or more. Default: empty.

list_mid.description:
Between the runs of a list, except before the last. Default: `${sep} `;
compact: `,`.

list_midlast.description: Before the last run of a list. Default: `${sep} ${and} `; compact: `,`.

list_post.description: After three runs or more. Default: empty.

empty.description:
The text written when there is no number at all, and the variable
`empty`. Default: `(empty)`.

JoinDecl.description:
The join texts of a counter style: the texts that join several numbers
into one text, such as `1–3, 7, and 9`.

Every field is a text written between or around the numbers, and each may
be left unset, in which case the default text is used (the defaults are
given per field below). The texts are FLM. A `${name}` in one of them is
replaced by the text of the key `name`, in one pass (a replaced text is not
scanned again); the keys meant for this use are the four variables `and`,
`sep`, `endash` and `empty`, so that a caller changes the word `and` once
instead of in every join text that uses it. A `${name}` whose name is not a key fails the
compilation of the counter style (`StyleError::UnknownVariable`).

Which fields are used depends on how many *runs* the numbers form, a run
being one number or a sequence of consecutive numbers:

- one run: `one_pre`, the run, `one_post`;
- two runs: `pair_pre`, the first, `pair_mid`, the second, `pair_post`;
- more: `list_pre`, the runs separated by `list_mid`, `list_midlast`
  before the last one, `list_post`.

A run of several numbers is written as `range_pre`, the first number, then
`range_pairmid` for a run of exactly two or `range_mid` for a longer one,
then the last number, then `range_post`.

The refs feature uses the same declaration for the texts that join the
targets of a reference to several targets.

userdefs.description: The user definitions (macros, environments and special character sequences defined by substitution), one map per kind, and the expansion depth limit. Fixed when the registry is built: it cannot vary per document or per render.

macros.description:
The macros: a map from a macro's name, without the backslash, to its
definition. The order written is kept.

environments.description:
The environments: a map from an environment's name to its definition.
The order written is kept.

specials.description:
The special character sequences: a map from the characters of a
sequence to its definition. The order written is kept.

recursion_limit.description:
The expansion depth limit: how many expansions one chain of use sites
may nest before a use site is reported with
`flm.userdefs.recursion-limit`. The default is 32
(`UserdefsConfig::recursion_limit`).

The macros: a map from a macro's name, without the backslash, to its
definition. The order written is kept.

environments.description:
The environments: a map from an environment's name to its definition.
The order written is kept.

specials.description:
The special character sequences: a map from the characters of a
sequence to its definition. The order written is kept.

The expansion depth limit: how many expansions one chain of use sites

`flm.userdefs.recursion-limit`. The default is 32

UserdefsData.description:
The settings of the `userdefs` feature as data gives them: the user
definitions in one map per kind, and the expansion depth limit.

The library reads the settings into this type and converts it to a
`UserdefsConfig` with `From`: the macros in the order written, then the
environments, then the special character sequences, each entry giving the
definitions that `DefinitionData::definitions` returns for it (one, or one
per parsing mode). The field documentation below is the description of each
settings key in the settings' JSON Schema.

args.description:
The arguments, in the order they are written at a use site. Each
argument gives its syntax as a structured syntax: a map whose key
`syntax` holds the name of a standard kind of argument and whose other
keys hold the kind's parameters, beside the argument's own keys
(`name`, `mode`, `layout`, `opaque_wrapper`, `scoped`, `docs`, `role`),
as in `{syntax: delimited-group, delimiters: ["(", ")"], name: size}`
for a group in parentheses named `size`. An argument code is a
shorthand for a structured syntax: in a map, the key `code` holds it in
place of `syntax`, so `{code: "r()", name: size}` declares the same
argument; a code alone (`"{"`) declares an argument with no other key.
The list is written in one of three shapes: one text in which each
character is one code (`"[{"`); a list of codes (`["[", "r()"]`); or a
list whose entries are each a code or a map. The kinds and their
parameters are listed in the documentation of the standard
kinds, and the codes
in the table of argument codes.

content.description:
The template: FLM text with placeholders, which replaces every use site.
One text is the template in text mode and in mathematics mode, and the
definition applies in each mode where the text parses. A map with the
keys `text` and `math`, one or both written, gives one template per
mode, and the definition applies in the modes written.

defaults.description:
The default values of the arguments: template text, keyed by the
argument's declared name or by the number a placeholder refers to it
by. A default value replaces the placeholders of an argument that a use
site leaves out.

argument_number_offset.description:
The argument number offset: how many of the first declared arguments
the numbered placeholders skip, so that `#1` refers to the argument at
this index (counting from zero).

block_role.description:
The block role of the definition's element: a block of its own, inline
content, or a block decorator.

expand.description:
When the use sites are expanded: `always`, in every plan, or `per-plan`
(the default), as each plan decides.

overrides.description:
Whether this definition replaces another feature's definition of the
same command. Without it, two features that define one command make the
registry build fail, unless the feature order places the feature
registered last explicitly after the other.

docs.description:
The definition's documentation, shown wherever the registry describes
its element.

DefinitionData.description:
A user definition as data gives it, under its name in the map of its kind
(`UserdefsData`): the fields of a `Definition` except its name, its
kind and its parsing modes, which the entry's name, the map and the content
give, and except its extra placeholders
(`Definition::extra_placeholder`), which only a definition declared in
Rust can have. A field not written keeps the value that
`Definition::new` gives it.

`definitions` returns the definitions the
entry declares, given its kind and its name. The field documentation below
is the description of each settings key in the settings' JSON Schema.

anyOf.description: One text in which each character is one argument code: `"[{{"`.
A list of arguments, each an argument code or a map.

ArgListData.description:
The argument list of a macro or environment declared in settings given as
data, written either as one text in which each character is one argument
code (`"[{"`), or as a list whose entries are each a code or an argument's
map (`ArgData`).

`arg_defs` converts it into argument declarations;
`deserialize_arg_list` reads a settings field of type `Vec<ArgDef>` in any
of the shapes. The module documentation describes the shapes and
the forms of an argument's syntax.

The argument's name, by which a user definition's template refers to
it. No name by default.

layout.description:
How the argument's content is laid out: `inline` (running text with
no paragraph, the default), `blocks` (paragraphs and other blocks), or
`inline-or-blocks` (decided by the content); see `ArgLayout`.

Whether the argument's content is placed under an opaque wrapper, so
that it is kept as written: no whitespace is collapsed and no
typographic substitution is made inside it. `false` by default; see

mode.description:
The parsing mode the argument is read in: `text` or `math`. Without

environment body declared `BodyLayout::Blocks`. Content written on
one line becomes one paragraph.

blank line (a paragraph break) or a block-level construct such as a
list, inline content otherwise. This is the rule a fragment laid out
`InlineOrBlocks`
applies to its top level.

ArgLayout.description:
How the block-structure pass lays out an
argument's content: as inline
content, as a region of blocks, or as whichever of the two the content
calls for.

Inline content is running text (words, formulas, commands such as
`\emph{…}`) with no paragraph inside it. A region of blocks holds
paragraphs and block-level constructs such as lists. The layout belongs to
the command's declaration (`ArgDef::layout`); an author cannot choose it
where the command is written.

An argument declared with an opaque wrapper (`ArgDef::opaque_wrapper`)
takes only `Inline`: the block-structure pass carries
its content over as written, so no other layout could take effect. An
argument read in mathematics mode is an opaque
region, which the
block-structure pass carries over untouched, so it may not be declared
`Blocks`. Minting reports a declaration that breaks
either rule
(`MintError::LayoutOnOpaqueWrappedArgument`,
`MintError::BlocksOnMathArgument`).
A layout declared on an argument whose reader yields raw text or places
its content under an opaque wrapper by construction (a verbatim argument, a
characters-only group) is not reported; it has no effect, since the
argument's content is an opaque region.

`arg_layout_of` returns the declared layout of an
argument of a parsed node;
`argument_holds_blocks`
returns whether an argument holds blocks, before and after the
block-structure pass alike.

BlockRole.description:
The role of an occurrence in the block and paragraph structure: a block,
inline content, or a block decorator.

The block-structure rewrite pass (`crate::lang::rewrites::blocks`) reads
it to cut content into blocks: the pass begins a new block at each `Block`
node and at each paragraph break, keeps `Inline` nodes inside the
surrounding block, and attaches a `BlockDecorator` to the block it occurs
in. When the pass trims the whitespace at the edges of a block, it looks
past a decorator, so a decorator at an edge does not keep the whitespace
beside it.

An element that declares no `BlockRoleAspect` has `BlockRole::DEFAULT`;
read an occurrence's role with `block_role_of`.

absorb_before.description: Remove the whitespace immediately before the element.

absorb_after.description: Remove the whitespace immediately after the element.

InlineSpacing.description:
How an inline element treats the whitespace immediately before and after
it: the data of `BlockRole::Inline`.

Setting either field removes the whitespace on that side entirely, so that
an element such as a citation mark can control its own spacing. The
whitespace removed is every piece of whitespace between the element and the
nearest content on that side, the nodes that are whitespace
(`Whitespace`, such as `~` and `\ `) included: before an element that
absorbs the whitespace before it, `word~`, `word ~ ` and `word~~` all leave
`word` alone. Source comments between the whitespace and the element do not
prevent the removal, and are kept: in `word %% note` followed on the next
line by the element, the space after `word` is removed too. Ordinary inline
content keeps the spaces around it: `InlineSpacing::CONTENT`.

oneOf.description:

content that follows it belongs to that block, as for a run-in heading.

Last in its block: the block ends after the element, as for the mark
that closes a proof.
Anywhere in its block; the element begins or ends no block.

Placement.description:
Where a block decorator is placed within its block: the data of
`BlockRole::BlockDecorator`.

A block decorator is an element attached to the block it occurs in, such as
a run-in heading or the mark that closes a proof. The block-structure pass
(`crate::lang::rewrites::blocks`) places it accordingly.

ExpandPolicy.description:

`per-plan`, as each plan decides.

The `flm.userdefs.expand-always` stage expands the `always` definitions in
every plan. The `flm.userdefs.expand` stage expands the `per-plan`
definitions in a plan that asks for expanded definitions
(`flm.userdefs.expanded`, the default choice); in a plan that asks for kept
definitions (`flm.userdefs.kept`), their use sites stay in the tree, and a
lowering rule either writes each one to the output as a call of the
definition or writes the instantiated template in its place.

PiecesRenderOptions.description:
The render option that chooses which declared pieces a render places,
beyond the defaults, and which of them each backend may place.

A render places every piece declared on by default
(`PieceDecl::default_on`)
that `exclude` does not list, and every piece `include` lists; a piece in
both sets is therefore placed. On a backend that has an entry in
`backends`, the render places only those of them the
entry lists. On a backend without an entry, it places those of them the
backend places by default: all of them, or none for a backend whose
pieces stage places only the pieces listed for it
(`PiecesStage::placing_only_named`).
`selected_pieces` is the only function that applies these rules.

The option is declared with `Bind::Render`: it is part of the render
request and of the plan key, since the pieces a render places decide
which builder stages the plan schedules. A piece left out schedules
nothing. The two sets apply to every backend of the render alike. A piece
name in them that no feature declares is reported
(`flm.pieces.unknown-piece`) and ignored.

text.description: the line width in columns (null: never wrap), default 80; the width of a tab in columns, default 4; the stop written after a run-in heading's title, default `.`, the empty text for none; whether a link to an address outside the document prints the address after its content, default on; whether a link whose content already shows its address prints the address too, default off; and the heading level printed as a first-level heading, default 1. Set per render request.

width.description: The line width in columns; `None` never wraps. The default is 80.

tab_width.description:
The width of a tab in columns: how far a line indented by one
tab (one `\indent`
in a lines section of a quotation) is indented. The default is 4. Every
length, in any unit, is converted to columns by
`columns`.

run_in_stop.description:
The stop written after the title of a run-in heading (a heading set at
the start of the paragraph it introduces), so that `\paragraph{Note} Some
content.` is printed as `Note. Some content.` The default is
`DEFAULT_RUN_IN_STOP`,
a period; the empty text writes no stop.

The stop is written only when the title does not already end in
sentence punctuation
(`ends_in_sentence_punctuation`).
That test looks only at the last characters of the title's text, so a
title ending in a formula, or in a symbol drawn by an author's own
command, gets the stop after it. A program that needs another treatment
of headings registers a lowering rule or a stage of its own (the
extension guide).

link_addresses.description:
Whether a link to an address outside the document prints that address
after its content, between angle brackets: `\href{https://example.com}{Click
here}` prints `Click here <https://example.com>`. The default is `true`.
Off, every link prints its content alone, which keeps a text holding
many links readable. A link to a place inside the document prints its
content alone either way.

link_addresses_when_shown.description:
Whether a link whose content already shows its address also prints the
address after it. A `\url` or an `\email` is such a link: its content
is derived from the address by the lowering rule that produced the
link, which sets
`LinkPayload::shows_target`.
With this option off (the default), `\url{https://example.com}` prints
`example.com`; on, it prints `example.com <https://example.com>`. It
has no effect when `link_addresses` is off.

root_heading_level.description:
The heading level the text output writes as its first-level heading.
A heading's level is a number counted from zero, smaller for an outer
heading
(`HeadingPayload::level`).
A heading at this level is underlined with `=`, a heading one level
deeper with `-`, and every deeper heading is preceded by `#`
characters, one
more than its depth below this level as
`heading_depth` counts
it from 0: three for a heading two levels below. The default is
`DEFAULT_ROOT_HEADING_LEVEL`,
1, the level of a section, the same as for the HTML backend's option of
the same name
(`HtmlRenderOptions::root_heading_level`).

A heading whose level is less than this one is reported as
`flm.pres.heading-above-root`
and written as a first-level heading. The option affects only the
underline or the `#` characters of a block heading: the numbering and the
run-in headings use a heading's own level.

width.description: The line width in columns; `None` never wraps. The default is 80.

tab_width.description:
The width of a tab in columns: how far a line indented by one
tab (one `\indent`
in a lines section of a quotation) is indented. The default is 4. Every
length, in any unit, is converted to columns by
`columns`.

run_in_stop.description:
The stop written after the title of a run-in heading (a heading set at
the start of the paragraph it introduces), so that `\paragraph{Note} Some
content.` is printed as `Note. Some content.` The default is
`DEFAULT_RUN_IN_STOP`,
a period; the empty text writes no stop.

The stop is written only when the title does not already end in
sentence punctuation
(`ends_in_sentence_punctuation`).
That test looks only at the last characters of the title's text, so a
title ending in a formula, or in a symbol drawn by an author's own
command, gets the stop after it. A program that needs another treatment
of headings registers a lowering rule or a stage of its own (the
extension guide).

link_addresses.description:
Whether a link to an address outside the document prints that address
after its content, between angle brackets: `\href{https://example.com}{Click
here}` prints `Click here <https://example.com>`. The default is `true`.
Off, every link prints its content alone, which keeps a text holding
many links readable. A link to a place inside the document prints its
content alone either way.

link_addresses_when_shown.description:
Whether a link whose content already shows its address also prints the
address after it. A `\url` or an `\email` is such a link: its content
is derived from the address by the lowering rule that produced the
link, which sets
`LinkPayload::shows_target`.
With this option off (the default), `\url{https://example.com}` prints
`example.com`; on, it prints `example.com <https://example.com>`. It
has no effect when `link_addresses` is off.
